As per letter dated 21/03/2017 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification No. L- 
26012/10/2016-(IR(M)) dt. 21/03/2017. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of Management in terminating the services of Shri Girdhari Sahu S/o Late Prahlad 
Sahu, Ex-Attendant, working in public Health Engg. Department of Bhilai Steel Plant on the ground of 
absenteeism and communicated through order T&/PHED/H/2015/288 dated 29-01-2015 is legal and 
justified? If not, what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


7084 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


Case of the Workman is that he was initially appointed in 2009 on the post of Attendant in Public Health 
Engineering Department of Management. He was terminated vide order of Management dated 29.01.2015 for the 
charge of unauthorized absence from his Workplace since March 2012 to May 2013. According to Workman, no full 
and proper opportunity was given to defend his case. It is also alleged that the charges have been wrongly held proved 
and the punishment is disproportionate to the charge. 


Case of the Management on this issue is that, the Workman was working as Attendant since 01.11.2009 he 
was habitual absentee, he had history of unauthorized absenteeism in which he was punished as many as three times 
but he did not improved. For the present charge, he admitted the charge during the enquiry. He was issued a show- 
cause notice on Enquiry Report before Awarding punishment. 


Management has filed photocopy enquiry papers which have been admitted by Workman. 
According to Management the charges have been accordingly held proved and the punishment is also 
proportionate to the misconduct proved. 
Following preliminary issues was framed on the basis of pleadings. 
1. Whether the Departmental Enquiry conducted against the Workman is legal? 
This issue was decided on the basis of evidence vide order dated 13.02.2025 holding the Departmental 
Enquiry legal and proper. This order is part of this Judgment. 
Following additional issues were framed thereafter — 
1. Whether the charges are proved? 
2. Whether the punishment is proportionate to the charge? 


Parties were given opportunity to lead evidences if any on these issues. No evidences were filed by any of 
the parties. I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for Workman Mr. Arun Patel and Learned Counsel Mr. R.C. 
Shrivastava for the Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


Additional Issue No. 1 — 


The settled preposition of law with respect to proof of charges in Departmental proceeding is that, the 
charges need not be proved beyond doubt as it is required in Criminal Trials, they are required to be proved to the 
extent of probability and possibility only. Now looking into the evidences collected during the enquiry, it comes out 
that, the absence of the Workman is not disputed during the enquiry. 


Case of the Workman is that, he was getting treatment on different station for some skin disease hence he 
could not inform the Management and could not attend his job. There is nothing on record in the enquiry papers to 
show that any document or any certificate by the Doctor had been produced during the enquiry or even before this 
Tribunal to show that during the period of absence in the charge sheet, the Workman was confined to bed and was 
advised bed rest. In absence of such evidence, the enquiry officer and competent authority cannot be held unjustified 
in recording finding that the absence of the Workman was willful, and unauthorized. Hence, the charges are held 
proved against the Workman. 


Additional Issue No.1 is answered accordingly. 
Additional Issue No.2 - 


On the basis of evidence during the enquiry, it comes that, workman has been in the habit of willful and 
unauthorizedly absenting himself from workplace in earlier years also and he was punished for this misconduct earlier 
also thrice in 2011, and once in 2012 & 2013. Keeping in view the fact that, he is a repeated offender, the punishment 
ordered is held not so disproportionate to shock the conscious of this Tribunal. Hence, holding the punishment not 
disproportionate to the charges to warrant interference this additional issue is answered accordingly. 


On the basis of above discussion and findings the reference is answered as follows. 
AWARD 


Holding the action of Management in terminating the services of Shri Girdhari Sahu S/o Late Prahlad 
Sahu, Ex-Attendant, working in public Health Engg. Department of Bhilai Steel Plant is not against law. He is 
entitled to no relief. 


No order as to cost. 
DATE:- 01/10/2025 
P.K. SRIVASTAVA, Presiding Officer

(JUDGMENT) 
(Passed on this 377 of October- 2025) 


As per letter dated 11/08/2014 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per 
Notification No. L-29012/9/2014-IR (M) dt. 11/08/2014. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of Bhilai Steel Plant, Iron Ore Complex, Dalli Rajhara, Distt- 
Balod in not correcting the date of birth of Sh. G. Satyam, Staff Attendant, (Personnel No. 990002) from 
05.07.1954 to 27.05.1959 is justified or not? If not, what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


Case of the applicant/Workman is mainly that he was first appointed as Head Cook in the statutory 
Canteen of the management company from 01.05.1978, his date of birth was recorded as 27.05.1959. On his 
regularization as Staff Attendant, he was posted as Staff Attendant in the Mines Organization of the management vide 
order dated 26.11.2009 in the Rajhara Mines, his date of birth was recorded in Form-B maintained by the Mines as 
27.05.1959 and was attested by Mines Manager, he had submitted his attestation Form dated 07.11.2009 containing 
his same date of birth i.e., 27.05.1959, attested by the Deputy General Manager (Mines), he had obtained his school 
leaving certificate dated 23.04.1966 from the school where he was first admitted. His same date of birth i.e., 
27.05.1959 was recorded in the certificate. The management arbitrarily changed his date of birth from 27.05.1959 to 
05.07.1954 in their record. He filed written representation on 08.09.2011 requesting the management to correct his 
date of birth as the mistake was detected by him only in the year 2011 but of no avail. He again filed a detailed 
representation on 08.05.2013 to the Chief Executive Officer, the General Manager Rajhara Mines and the General 
Manager (Personnel) through proper channel. This representation was also not heard of and no action was taken. He 
raised dispute in this respect before the Assistant Labour Commissioner, the Union also raised the dispute in this 
respect after failure of conciliation, the reference was made to this Tribunal. 


In the meanwhile, the management superannuated him on the basis of his incorrect date of birth 05.07.1954. 
According to the workman, the action of changing date of birth of the workman by the management is unjust, illegal, 
malafide and arbitrary. Subsequently, the action of management in superannuating him on the basis of his changed 
date of birth is also arbitrary and illegal. The workman has requested that holding the action of management in 
unilaterally changing his date of birth from 27.05.1959 to 05.07.1954, unjust, illegal and arbitrary, the action of 
management in superannuating the workman on the basis of changed date of birth 05.07.1954 be held unjust, illegal 
and arbitrary. Further, he be held entitled to be reinstated and entitled to all consequential pre as well post retiral 
benefits, deeming him in service till the date of his superannuation based on his date of birth 27.05.1959. 


The case of the management is mainly that, the workman was appointed as Head Cook on 01.05.1978 by 
Employees New Cooperative Canteen. Subsequently, he was appointed as Attendant in Bhilai Steel Plant in grade S-1 
vide offer letter dated 28.10.2009, he joined on 01.11.2009. He was placed in Rajhara Mines on 05.12.2009, in 
connection with order of Hon’ble High Court of M.P., Jabalpur in L.P.A. No. 208 & 209 of 1995 a detail information 
was collected from all the cooperative canteens in the year 1996. The President, Coke Oven Cooperative Society 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7087 


Canteen submitted list of canteen workers working in the Coke Oven Cooperative Canteen in the prescribed format 
showing the date of birth of the workman as 05.07.1954. On the basis of this list, the canteen workers in the list were 
subjected to medical examination, the date of birth of the workman was mentioned as 05.07.1954 in the medical 
examination, based on declaration made by him. The workman submitted declaration Form with respect to dependant 
family members for free medical treatment in which he had declared his age as 56 years on 17.11.2011 which nears to 
1954, he put his signature on that Form. 


It is further the case of the management that the workman did not submit any record with respect to his 
educational qualification/ date of birth, etc. The CPF declaration & nomination submitted before Coke Oven 
Cooperative Canteen by the workman prior to absorption in the Bhilai Steel Plant shows his date of birth 05.07.1954. 
The retirement age of employees working in the management is 60 years, the workman was issued retirement notice 
dated 31.05.2014 and he has been superannuated on the basis of his date of birth 05.07.1954 vide order of 
management effective from 31.07.1954. Thus according to management, Form-B Register, Service Register, 
Attestation Form, CPF declaration and nomination Form and Medical Examination Certificate mentions his date of 
birth as 05.07.1954 which he was very well aware of, he raised the dispute in this respect at fag end of its service, the 
management has thus requested that the reference be answered against the workman. 


The Workman has filed his rejoinder wherein he has stated that the so called list sent by the President does 
not bear the signature of workman, hence he is not responsible for any entry in the list which was not prepared by him 
nor was counter signed by him. He has mainly reiterated his allegation taken in his statement of claim. 


Case No. A-01/2014 has been filed by the applicant/workman under section 33-A of the Act, challenging the 
same order of management with regard to his superannuation on the basis of his date of birth 05.07.1954, on the 
ground that it is in violation of section 33-A of the Act with almost the same allegations. Management has also filed 
its written reply with almost the same pleadings taken by them in case No. R-75/2014 


Since the parties, the facts and dispute in both the cases are similar, hence vide order dated 14.12.2015 
passed by my learned predecessor, both the cases were consolidated and case No. R-75/2014 has been made 
leading case. 


In evidence, the workman has filed his affidavit as his Examination-in-chief, he has been cross-examined by 
management. 


The President of the Union has also filed his affidavit as his Examination-in-chief. He has also been cross- 
examined by management. 


The workman has filed and proved his original appointment letter dated 01.05.1978, certificate issued by the 
Manager of canteen dated 05.11.2005 CPF declaration and nomination Form dated 11.06.1999 with respect to 
Cooperative Canteen, RTI obtained document, attestation Form, Form-B prepared in Rajhara Mines, CPF declaration 
Form in Rajhara Mines, medical examination record in Rajhara Mines, documents which are representations and 
replies during conciliation proceedings before Labour Commissioner. 


Management has filed affidavit of its witness Rohit Kumar, Personnel Officer as his Examination-in-chief, 
has also filed and proved letter of Manager, P. Panigrahi canteen dated 17.05.1996, asking the President, Coke Oven 
Cooperative Society Canteen to furnish information with respect to persons employed in the canteen in compliance of 
order of Hon’ble High Court, letter of President with list, list of canteen workers for medical examination, declaration 
with respect to dependants for free treatment, CPF declaration and nomination Form. 


It is also worth mention here that, the workman died during the pendency of the proceeding, his legal 
representatives have been substituted in his place. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for the Workman Mr. Arun Patel and Mr. R. C. Shrivastava, 
Learned Counsel for the Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


On perusal of record in light of rival arguments, the reference itself is the issue for determination. 


Pleadings of the parties have already been detailed earlier, the workman side has corroborated its case, as 
stated above, in workman affidavit as his Examination-in-chief, he has stated that he was first appointed as head cook 
on 01.05.1978 his date of birth was recorded on 27.05.1959 in his service record at the time of his appointment his 
service were regularized and thereafter he was appointed as Staff Attendant w.e.f., 26.11.2009, the management 
altered his date of birth in his service record without his consent and changed it from 27.05.1959 to 05.07.1954, which 
is illegal on the part of management and has superannuated him on the basis of his changed date of birth. He has 
proved Form-B Ex-W/1 maintained by Rajhara Mines after his confirmation which bears his date of birth 27.05.1959, 
he has further proved Attestation Form prepared during his first service i.e., Coke Oven Cooperative Society where he 
was appointed as Head Cook, this form also contains his date of birth 27.05.1959, he has further filed his school 
leaving certificate and proved it as Ex-W/3 which contain his date of birth 27.05.1959. 


7088 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


He has further filed and proved various communications made by the Labour Commissioner with respect to 
his representations regarding correction of his date of birth which are Ex-W/5 to Ex-W/11. In his cross-examination 
he has stated that he studied in school till class Second regarding the document of management which is signed and 
prepared by the President of the Canteen Society which is list of the canteen workers and CPF declaration and 
nomination Form Ex-M/1 and Ex-M/2. He has stated that his signatures on these forms have not been done by him. 


The President of the workman union has also examined himself by way of filing his affidavit as his 
Examination-in-chief, he has also been examined by management. His statements corroborate the statement of the 
workman 


The management witness has corroborated the case of the management in his statement on oath as his 
Examination-in-chief, he has stated that the workman was first appointed as head cook on 01.05.1978 by Employees 
Cooperative Canteen Cook Oven, he was subsequently appointed as Attendant in Bhilai Steel Plant vide letter dated 
28.10.2009, he joined on 01.11.2009 and was posted in Rajhara Mines where he joined on 05.12.2009 under order of 
Hon’ble High Court, President of the Canteen Union submitted his recommendation containing list of employee 
workers in the canteen which contained name of the applicant/workman, also his date of birth was mentioned as 
05.07.1954 in that list. The workman mentioned his same date of birth i.e., 05.07.1954 in his declaration form 
regarding dependant family members mentioning his age as 56 years as on 17.11.2011 which corresponds to 1954 and 
put his signature, he did not submitted any document regarding his educational qualification, the CPF declaration and 
nomination submitted by him before Coke Oven Cooperative Canteen also contained his date of birth as 05.07.1954, 
he was superannuated on his date of birth 05.07.1954 after attaining 60 years of age, he was well aware regarding his 
date of birth 05.07.1954 recorded in documents maintained by the management. He could not produce any reliable 
document with regard to his date of birth 27.05.1959 as claimed by him, management witness has proved these 
documents mentioned above.. 


On the basis of comparative analysis of the documentary as well statements on behalf of the parties, it comes 
out that undisputedly, the date of birth of the workman where he was first employed was recorded as 27.05.1959. The 
same date of birth was recorded in Form-B at Rajhara Mines after his regularization. The Attestation Form filed by 
him while he was posted in Rajhara Mines, also contains the same date of birth 27.05.1959, his school leaving 
certificate also contains the same date of birth. In his first document regarding his appointment, he has made his 
signature, hence he cannot be said to be illiterate. The first document containing his changed date of birth as 
01.05.1954 is the list of employees prepared by the Coke Oven Cooperative Society Canteen, this list was not 
prepared by the workman, hence he cannot be held responsible for any entry regarding the date of birth in the list 
since the person who prepared the list and filed has not been examined by management, it cannot be said that on what 
basis he mentioned date of birth of the workman as 01.05.1954 whereas at that time the service records of the 
workman contained his date of birth as 27.05.1959. Thereafter, in Form-B Register maintained by management, 
Service Register, Attestation Form, CPF declaration and nomination Form his date of birth 05.07.1954 is mentioned, 
the medical declaration form does not contain date of birth of the workman rather it contain his approximate age at 
time of filling form i.e., 17.11.2011, the CPF declaration and nomination Form Ex-M/1 does not contain the signature 
of the workman, there is overwriting in the column of date of birth which has been prepared on 01.06.1990. 


It is apparent from the date mentioned on it, the CPF declaration and nomination Form filed and proved by 
the workman which is 15.03.2010 contains date of birth of the workman as 27.05.1959. Similarly, the Form-B of the 
workman does not contain the date of its preparation. Attestation Form prepared on 07.11.2009 contained the date of 
birth of the workman as 27.05.1959. Thus, it is established that there are two sets of documents with the management 
containing two sets of dates of birth of the workman. In such a situation, it was incumbent on the management to 
enquire into this controversy and settle it. The case of the management and submission of the Learned Counsel on this 
point is that the workman himself signed his date of birth in the records maintained by management, which contained 
his date of birth as 05.07.1954. We will have to look into first declaration with respect to date of birth of the workman 
which was made by him at the time of his first appointment in 1978. It may be taken as most accurate, those date of 
birth declared is 27.05.1959. 


It comes out that the date of birth of the workman 05.07.1954 crept for the first time in the list prepared by 
the President and thereafter it was entered into some of the records of the management after the workman was granted 
permanent status. 


It has been submitted from the side of management that the workman accepted his changed date of birth and 
now started agitating against this at fag end of his career just before his superannuation which is not permitted in law. 
Learned Counsel has referred to Single Bench of Hon’ble High Court of M.P. in the case of Surendra Singh vs. State 
of M.P., 2007 (1) MPLJ 286, in this case the workman filed application for correction of his date of birth after 32 
years of service, which he was not permitted. In another case State of U.P. vs. Shivnarayan Upadhyaya, (2005) 6 
SCC 49, referred to by Learned Counsel for management, when the entry regarding date of his birth was challenged 
by the workman on the eve of retirement, Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that Courts and Tribunals should be slow 
in issuing direction for correction of date of birth unless there is clinching and unimpeachable evidence in this regard. 
Also held that in such cases, challenge to date of birth should normally not be entertained when they are made at the 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7089 


eve of retirement. In another reported decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court, in the case of Union of India vs. Harnam 
Singh, (1993) 2 SCC 162, it has been held that when a limitation for seeking change in date of birth is provided, 
claims barred by limitation, should not be entertained except for valid reasons. 


The referred cases can be distinguished on facts. In the case in hand, the workman has been consistently 
agitating for correction of his date of birth. 


Learned Counsel for workman has relied on judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Sarjoo 
Prasad v/s General Manager & Anr., Case No. 377/1981, SCC 544. In this case the Hon’ble Supreme Court has 
referred to and relied on this judgment in the case of State of Orissa v/s Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei & Ors., AIR 1967 
SC 1269 and has held that date of birth of employee, once accepted by employer cannot be altered without giving him 
an opportunity of hearing and has further held the superannuation of the employee on the basis of his altered date of 
birth against law. The same view has been taken by Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Hari Singh v/s State of 
Bihar, 2000 SC (L & S) 832, proposition of law laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court in these referred cases will apply 
in the case in hand. 


On the basis of above discussion, action of the management of Bhilai Steel Plant, in altering the date of birth 
of the workman Gowdi Satyam from 27.05.1959 to 05.07.1954 and superannuating him on the basis of his altered 
date of birth, is held without authority and in violation of law. Consequently, the workman is held entitled to be 
reinstated from the date he was superannuated by the management and to be deemed in service till the date of 
superannuation on the basis of his date of birth 27.05.1959 with all back wages and pre as well post retiral benefits, 
payable to his legal representatives, by management within 30 days from the date of publication of award, failing 
which interest @ 6% per annum from the date of award till payment. 


On the basis of above discussion and findings, the reference deserves to be answered as follows:- 
AWARD 


Holding the action of management of Bhilai Steel Plant, Iron Ore Complex, Dalli Rajhara, Distt- Balod in 
not correcting the date of birth of Sh. (८ Satyam, Staff Attendant, from 05.07.1954 to 27.05.1959 is against law and 
arbitrary. He is entitled to be reinstated from the date from which he was superannuated by the management and to 
be deemed in service till the date of superannuation on the basis of his date of birth 27.05.1959 with all back wages 
and pre as well post retiral benefits, payable to his legal representatives, by management, within 30 days from the 
date of publication of award, failing which interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of award till payment. 


Connected case No. A-01/2014 also stands disposed accordingly. 
No order as to cost. 
DATE:- 03/10/2025 
P.K. SRIVASTAVA, Presiding Officer

Sh. K.K Pandey, Ld. AR along with Sh. Shivram Aggarwal (MW) for management M-5 i.e. Prominent 


Housekeeping. 
AWARD 
07.11.2025 
1. This is an application under section 2A of the 1.0 Act (hereinafter referred as an ‘Act’) filed by the 


claimant stating that he was working as Supervisor and presently deployed at MMTC having its office at Scope 
Complex, Lodhi Colony, New Delhi. Respondent no. 5 is the outsourced agency. Outsourced employed have been 
paid less than the minimum wages. Respondent no. 2 & 3 are the employees of the Respondent no. | and they are 
involved in unfair labour practices. Respondent no. 2 & 3 were forcibly taking Rs. 4,000/- in cash from each deployed 
outsourced employees and further they are getting the sign on the receipt of Rs. 13,500/-. Claimant has raised his 
voice. However, instead of taking action, he was got transferred at MMTC go-down at Jhandewalan. It is further his 
case that he has been deployed as Supervisor at the MMTC office through the Prominent House Keeping agency 1.6. 
Respondent no. 5 and he has been discharging his duties and responsibility with utmost honesty and sincerity. One 
Rahul remained absent and he was instructed to perform his duty as per the roaster, failing which conduct of him shall 
be reported to the owner of the Housekeeping Agency. According to him his transfer was a punishment order and was 
done under the influence of the Respondent no. 2 & 3. When the workman went for joining at Manesar, it is utter 
shock to workman when he was not allowed to enter the premises and not allow to join the services. He further 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7091 


submitted that he is still under the employment of the respondent management. They fail to make the payment of June 
2018 to till date. He made prayer that award be passed of the amount of Rs. 2,72,000/- and direct the management to 
join his duty at MMTC at Lodhi Colony. 


2. Management no. 1, 2, 3 & 4 have already been proceeded exparte vide order dated 27.04.2022. 
Management-5 has filed its written statement stating that application filed by the claimant is prima facie, 
misconceived, devoid of any justification and jurisdiction. He further submitted that claim is not maintainable as the 
claimant was working with the respondent in a capacity of Supervisor and he was deployed at one of the clients of the 
respondent. The duties of the claimant was to manage and regulate day-to-day affairs of the answering respondent 
with his team, preparing duty rosters allocating duties and shifts for subordinates and takes decision independently to 
satisfy the client of the respondent who were engaged by the answering respondent and performing their duty under 
supervision and control of the claimant. He was authorized to assign the duty to the employees who were working 
under him, he was also authorized to sanction leave to his subordinate. The duties performed by the claimant being 
educative, creative administrative, managerial, supervisory, imaginative in nature thus the claimant do not fall within 
the prescribed categories laid down in section 2(s) of the Act. He also submitted that claim filed by the claimant is not 
maintainable as the claimant did not work for the respondent for a period of 240 days in a calendar year. He submitted 
that claim filed by the claimant is liable to be dismissed. 


3. Claimant has filed the rejoinder denying the averment made by the management in his written statement and 
affirmed the facts made in his claim statement. 

4. After completion of the pleadings vide order dated 13.04.2023, following issues have been framed: 

(1) Whether the proceeding is maintainable. 

(1) Whether the claimant is a workman as defined under section 2(s) of the 1.10 Act. 


(1) Whether the claimant had worked for 240 days in a calendar year preceeding to his alleged termination. 


(IV) Whether the service of the claimant was illegally terminated by the managements. 
(V) To what other relief the parties entitled to, and from whom and from which date? 
5. In order to prove its claim, claimant had tendered his affidavit in evidence affirming the facts made in his 


claim statement stating that he was working as a Supervisor. He was cross-examined where he admitted that he was 
appointed by prominent housekeeping i.e. M-5 on 02.07.2018 and performed his duty till 31.03.2019. He admitted 
that he was working in the capacity of supervisor and there were 23 to 25 Safai Karamchari staffs including one 
female workman were working under his supervision. 


6. Examination in chief and cross-examination of the witness has also been recorded. 


7. I have heard the argument at par. After going through the testimony of this witness, this tribunal has noticed 
that the claimant has nowhere mentioned that he was a workman either in his claim statement or in the affidavit of 
evidence. The claimant who was present himself admitted that he was a Supervisor and his job was to supervise the 
workmen. 


8. To invoke the jurisdiction of this tribunal, first the claimant has to assert that he was a workman within the 
definition of Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Section 2(s) is required to be reproduced herein: 


2 [(s) “workman” means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any manual, 
unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the terms 
of employment be express or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding under this Act in relation to an 
industrial dispute, includes any such person who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection 
with, or as a consequence of, that dispute, or whose dismissal, discharge or retrenchment has led to that 
dispute, but does not include any such person— 


(i) who is subject to the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), or the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950), or the Navy 
Act, 1957 (62 of 1957); or 


(ii) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison; or 


(iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity; or (iv) who, being employed in a 
supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding 3 [ten thousand rupees] per mensem or exercises, either by the 
nature of the duties attached to the office or by reason of the powers vested in him, functions mainly of a 
managerial nature.] 


9. Definition of the workman as provided U/s 2(s) is wide enough to include any person as workman in respect 
of his earning, however, section has itself carved out the exception as Clause-(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). The as exception 
stated that, the person who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison is excluded 
from the category of the workman. The 4" exception stated that, person being employed in a supervisory capacity, 
drawing wages exceeding Rs. 10,000/- per month is excluded from the category of the workman. 


7092 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


10. Claimant has filed the claim under section 2-A of the LD. Act stating that he was transferred to 
Manesar, Gurgaon and not allowing him to join the duty at Manesar amounts to termination. In the entire claim, 
claimant claims to be a supervisor and 23 to 25 Safari Karamchari staffs including one female were working under his 
supervision. 

11. From the averment made in the claim as well as in his affidavit, it appears that the claimant is not a 
workman as defined in the Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Nowhere has he mentioned either in his 
affidavit or in his claim petition that he had been given designation of Supervisor only by namesake and he was 
working as a workman. He admitted that his job profile was to inspect the work of cleaning staff. 


12. In view of the above discussion, Issue no. 1 & 2 are decided against the claimant and in favour of 
management. 
13. In view of the findings in issue no. 1 & 2, there is no need to decide issue no. 3 & 4. Claim of the claimant 


stands dismissed. Award is accordingly passed. A copy of this award be sent to the appropriate government for 
notification U/S 17 of the I.D Act. File is consigned to record room. 


Date: 07.11.2025 
ATUL KUMAR GARG, Presiding Officer

AWARD 


The Central Government, Ministry of Labour& Employment vide its Order No. M/.7/01/2022-B4/Adj/A1 
dated 25.11.2022 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“Whether the demand of Shri M.P. Musammil, Ex-LIC Development Officer for re-instatement or re- 
appointment with back wage into the service of LIC is justified ? If not, to what relief he is entitled to? 


2: ID called out. Heard of maintainability. Having gone through the record and after hearing the petitioner in 
person and representative of the Respondent / Management, the question that arises to consider at this stage is 
whether the petitioner / claimant comes under the category of workman. 


3. Q.1. The claimant filed a case law in LIC of India & Ors Vs. L. Shan Prasad in WA No.1159 of 2025 dated 
30.11.2025 and stated that, as per the decision of this case, he must be considered as a workman. On perusal of the 
judgment (supra) it reveals that the Hon’ble High Court of Kerala has nowhere discuss the defination of workman and 
that Development Officer comes under the category of the workman or not. The clear case law on the subject is 
Chauharya Tripathi & Ors Vs LIC of India & Ors wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that the Development 
Officers working in LIC are not workmen under Section 2(s) of the Industrial Dispute Act. 


4. In view of the judgment rendered by the Hon’ble Supreme Court, the claimant is not a workman, and 
therefore, this Tribunal has no jurisdiction to decide the lis. 

5. ID is dismissed in for want of jurisdiction and the reference is answered accordingly. 

6. The Petitioner / Claimant may file a petition before the competent authority, if so advised. 


SUSHIL KUMAR-IIL, Presiding Officer

AWARD 


The Central Government, Ministry of Labour& Employment vide its Order No.L-12011/11/2022-IR(B-1) 
dated 10.03.2022 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“Whether raising the issue of 17 charter of demands by the Tamil Nadu Grama Bank Officers’ Association and Tamil 
Nadu Grama Bank Workers Union against the management of Tamil Nadu Grama Bank, Salem are just & fair? If yes, 
what relief the workmen are entitled to?” 


2 On receipt of the above reference dated 10.03.2022 from the appropriate Government, the dispute was 
registered as ID No. 18/2022 and due notices were issued to both the parties for their appearance fixing the case to 
02.05.2022. On 02.05.2022 petitioner filed only Vakalat Nama resulting further adjournments to 11.07.2022, 
01.03.2023, 18.05.2023 and 19.07.2023. The Petitioner did not turn up whereas the 2™ Party / Respondent filed 
Vakalat Nama. It reveals from the body of reference that while the appropriate Govt. sent the reference dated 
10.03.2022 to this Tribunal for adjudication, copies of the reference were sent to the Petitioner and all the opposite 
parties. It is therefore well presumed that both parties must have received the reference. Even then, in the interest of 
justice, the Petitioner was once again directed to appear and to file claim statement fixing the case to 30.06.2025, 
18.08.2025 and 15.10.2025. The Petitioner did not turn and the claim statement was not furnished in any manner by 
the Petitioner. It reveals the Petitioner, despite of sufficient opportunity choose not to appear or to file claim 
statement and documents. 


3. In the circumstance it deems proper not to re-list the case for the same purpose to any other date which 
would be wastage of the valuable time of this Tribunal. The case was reserved for Final Order. 


4. In view of the discussion held supra, it is crystal clear that the petitioner has got no interest to proceed with 
the case. Thus, the Tribunal is not in a position to adjudicate the dispute as referred by the Appropriate Government, 
as there exists no Industrial Dispute for adjudication as per the reference. 


5. In the result the reference is answered against the petitioner. 
An Award is passed accordingly. 
SUSHIL KUMAR-I, Presiding Officer

(JUDGMENT) 
(Passed on this 03th day of October - 2025) 


As per letter dated 09/01/2012 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 
No. L-12011/69/2011-(IR(B-D) dt. 09/01/2012. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the demand of the Union for Payment of Bonus to Shri Mohd. Firdaus Sheikh for the period 
from 01/11/1988 to 31/03/2009, is legal and justified? To what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


Case of the Workman is that, he was first engaged as a Peon on daily wager by the Bank on 01.11.1988 and 
worked till June, 1996, when disengaged without any notice or compensation. He raised a dispute against his 
disengagement before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Bhopal. A settlement was made between him 
and the Bank on 13.02.1997 in which the Bank agreed to engage again him as a Daily wager. The Workman was 


7104 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


engaged by Bank as a daily wager. The reference was also made with respect to the dispute raised by him against his 
this disengagement which was registered as R/69/1998. The Workman raised a dispute on 15.09.2019 with respect to 
payment of bonus to him for the period he worked as a daily wager with the Bank. The Management disengaged him 
from 06.12.2009. According to the Workman though he worked from 01.11.1988 to 06.12.2009 he was not paid any 
bonus by the Bank. This action of Bank is unjust, illegal and arbitrary and is in violation of Section 8 and 11 of the 
Payment of Bonus Act. The Workman has prayed that he be held entitled to payment of Bonus for the period claimed 
by him. 


Case of Management is mainly that his claim for payment of bonus from 01.11.1988 to 31.03.2009 is 
barred by Payment of Bonus Act. Management has also denied that Workman has worked with the Management as 
claimed by him and has stated that the Workman had made same claim before the Considering Authority under 
minimum wages Act which was rejected by him, vide order dated 13.05.2013 on the ground that he failed to prove 
that he worked in the Bank from June, 2009 to December, 2009. The Bank has thus prayed that reference be answered 
against the Workman. 


In evidence, the Workman has filed his affidavit as his examination in chief. He has been cross-examined by 
Management. He has filed photocopy documents which are Ex. W-1 Copy of Notification and Messenger, Ex. W-2 
Copy of Application of Workman before Assistant Labour Commissioner, Ex. W-3 and W-5 are different 
representations made by the Workman. Ex. W-6 and W-7 are different payment vouchers paid to the Workman as 
alleged by him, Ex. W-8 is the reference with respect to regularization of the Workman, Ex. W-9 to W-28 are 
different communications made by Bank sending the Workman as Messenger at different places. Ex. W-24 to W-27 
are again payment vouchers, Ex. W-28 is RTI reply. 


Management has examined its witness Manoj Verma by way of filing his affidavit as his examination in 
chief. He has been cross-examined by Workman side. 


There is on record Photocopy of Judgment & Award dated 06.07.2015 in case R/69/1998 relating to 
regularization of the Workman and relating to termination of the services of the Workman w.e.f. 15.12.2009 relating 
to case R/82/2011. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel Mr. Arun Patel for the Workman and Mr. Subh Chaudhaha for 
Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


Reference itself is the issue for determination. 


Section 13, 14, 8, 10 and 22 of the Act are being reproduced as follows : - 
Section 8: Eligibility for bonus.— 


“Every employee shall be entitled to be paid by his employer in an accounting year, bonus, in accordance 
with the provisions of this Act, provided he has worked in the establishment for not less than thirty working days in 
that year.” 


Section 10. Payment of minimum bonus.— 


“Subject to the other provisions of this Act, every employer shall be bound to pay to every employee in 
respect of the accounting year commencing on any day in the year 1979 and in respect of every subsequent 
accounting year, a minimum bonus which shall be 8.33 per cent. of the salary of wage earned by the employee during 
the accounting year or one hundred rupees, whichever is higher, whether or not the employer has any allocable 
surplus in the accounting year: Provided that where an employee has not completed fifteen years of age at the 
beginning of the accounting year, the provisions of this section shall have effect in relation to such employees as if for 
the words “one hundred rupees”, the words “sixty rupees” were substituted.” 


Section 13. Proportionate reduction in bonus in certain cases.— 


“Where an employee has not worked for all the working days in an accounting year, the minimum bonus of 
one hundred rupees or, as the case may be, of sixty rupees, if such bonus is higher than 8.33 per cent. of his salary or 
wage for the days he has worked in that accounting year, shall be proportionately reduced.” 


Section 14. Computation of number of working days.— 


“For the purposes of section 13, an employee shall be deemed to have worked in an establishment in any 
accounting year also on the days on which— 


(a) he has been laid off under an agreement or as permitted by standing orders under the Industrial 
Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 (20 of 1946), or under the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 (14 of 1947), or under any other law applicable to the establishment; 


(b) he has been on leave with salary or wage; 


(c) he has been absent due to temporary disablement caused by accident arising out of and in the 
course of his employment; and 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7105 


(d) the employee has been on maternity leave with salary or wage, during the accounting year.” 


Section 22. Reference of disputes under the Act.— 


“Where any dispute arises between an employer and his employees with respect to the bonus payable 
under this Act or with respect to the application of this Act to an establishment in public sector, then, such dispute 
shall be deemed to be an industrial dispute within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947), or 
of any corresponding law relating to investigation and settlement of industrial disputes in force in a State and the 
provisions of that Act or, as the case may be, such law, shall, save as otherwise expressly provided, apply 
accordingly”. 


From perusal of these provisions, it is established that firstly, the Workman will be an ‘employee’ and 
Bank is an ‘employer’ within the Act even if the Workman succeeded in proving that he was a daily wager and 
worked with the Bank and secondly, that there is a dispute on the point whether the Workman is entitled to bonus as 
claimed by him which is the subject of the reference in the present case, hence the limitation under Section 21 of the 
Act will not apply in this case. The limitation will apply only when the Management is held under obligation to pay 
certain amount of bonuses to the Workman. 


The judgments and Awards passed by this Tribunal in the aforementioned cases R/69/1998 and 1२/82/2011 
and his disengagement by Bank vide order dated 15.12.2009 was also held unjust and he was directed to be reinstated 
in service with 50% back wages. There is nothing on record to show that these Judgments and Awards have been set- 
aside or modified by any Court or Tribunal. Hence, the findings of the Tribunal with regard to working period of the 
Workman with the Bank in these two cases will operate as res judicata. 


In the light of findings recorded in these two reference cases particularly in Case R/69/1988 in Para 11 of 
the judgment where it is proved that a Workman worked from 1988 to 1996 and again from 1997 to 2009, the action 
of Bank in not awarding him bonus for the period is held unjust and illegal on the part of the Management and the 
Workman is held to be entitled to bonuses from the Management Bank for this period. 


In the light of aforesaid discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows. 
AWARD 


Holding the demand of the Union for Payment of Bonus to Shri Mohd. Firdaus Sheikh for the period 
from 01/11/1988 to 31/03/2009, is legal and justified on the part of the Management and the Workman is held to be 
entitled to bonus from the Management Bank for this period. 


No order as to cost. 
DATE:- 03/10/2025 
P.K. SRIVASTAVA, Presiding Officer

The Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), Chennai, (Ministry of Labour & Employment) vide 
its Order No. M.No.8/10/2019-Al dated 18.12.2019 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for 
adjudication. 


2. The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“Whether the demand of Ms. J.Sasikala for reinstatement along with all benefits against the management 
of Department of Postal Accounts and Finance is legal and justified? If not, to what relief the concerned 
workwoman is entitled to?” 


3 As per the claim statement, the case of the Petitioner is that she entered as casual labourer in the 
2™ Party/Management and was engaged against MTS vacancy. She performed her duties of weeding out, arranging 
old records, maintaining office premises, gardening and scavenging. The Petitioner was engaged in the year 2004 and 
as per instructions of Department of Post vide letter No.65-24/88-SPB-I dated 17.05.1989, she is entitled to 
absorption as MTS, since she has completed 14 years service as casual labourer. However, the Petitioner was denied 
work from May, 2018. Therefore, the action of the respondent/Management in removing the Petitioner from service 
without any order, notice amounts to violation of principles of natural justice u/s.25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947. Therefore, it is prayed that Respondent may be directed to reinstate the Petitioner into service with a direction 
to absorb her on regular basis with back wages and other attendant benefits. 


4. In the counter statement, the Respondent stated that Petitioner is only a casual employee and at no point of 
time, there was employer-employee relationship. The Petitioner was engaged as an outsider for short spells in 
respect of housekeeping and allied duties on daily wage basis and against any MTS vacancy. No order of 
appointment or engagement was issued to the Petitioner. The casual labourers in employment up to 01.09.1993 
were only eligible to be conferred with temporary status. The Petitioner was neither engaged through employment 
exchange nor for any regular work or against any regular vacancy and is not possessing requisite eligibility criteria 


[भाग --खण्ड 3(ii)] 


for consideration against MTS post. 


भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7107 


The wages to the Petitioner were paid as per recommendations of District 


Collectorate. The same was drawn and paid as per envisaged norms from time to time. Therefore, the Petitioner is 
not entitled to any relief and the claim of the Petitioner is liable to be dismissed.

5. The Petitioner has submitted proof of affidavit in support of her claim and adduced oral evidence as WW1 
and documents filed by her were marked as Ex.W1 to W17. The Respondent has also filed its proof of affidavit 
and Shri R.Swaminathan, Assistant Chief Accounts Officer was examined as MWI1 and documents on behalf of 
respondent were marked as Ex.M1 to M7. 


6. Heard the learned counsel appearing for either side and perused the records. The point that arises for 
consideration is “whether the employee of the Respondent is entitled for reinstatement into service along with all 
benefits against the management of Department of Postal Accounts & Finance? If not to what relief the concerned 
workman is entitled?” 


7. The Petitioner Mrs. J.Sasikala has stated in her claim statement that she had entered into service of the 
Respondent in the year 2004. The fact of continuous service is established by the Petitioner by adducing oral 
evidence as WW1 and filing proof of affidavit and the documents which were marked as Ex.W1 to W17. 


8. The Respondent in its reply admitted this fact that Petitioner was engaged with the Department, but stated 
that engagement was on daily wage basis and not against any MTS vacancies. The Petitioner was not a permanent 
employee and there was no employer-employee relationship exists between the Respondent and the Petitioner. The 
Respondent further stated that no appointment or engagement order was issued to the Petitioner and as per circular 
dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995, casual labourers in employment upto 01.09.1993 were only eligible to be 
conferred with temporary status and the Petitioner was not working on 01.09.1993 with the Department and 
therefore, they are not entitled for any absorption. 


9. The learned counsel for the Respondent further submits that Multi Tasking Staff Recruitment Rules, 2010 
dated 12.12.2010 is not applicable to the Petitioner. As per circular dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995 the following 
conditions must be fulfilled:- 


a) Temporary status on or before 01.09.1993; 
b) Full time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993 & 
c) Part-time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993. 


10. The learned counsel for the Respondent contended that Petitioner was not engaged through employment 
exchange and no appointment letter was issued. He further stated that assumption of the Petitioner that he/she works 
against the post of MTS is incorrect. The learned counsel further stated that there was no relationship of employer- 
employee between the Respondent and Petitioner, hence the question of notice or protection u/s.25F of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947 does not arise. 


11. On behalf of the Respondent a circular dated 17.05.1989 has been filed which is marked as Ex.M1, and it 
clarifies the position of casual labourers and part-time casual labourers in para 2, which reads as under:- 


“2. It is hereby clarified that all daily wagers working in Post Offices or in RMS Offices or in Administrative 
Offices or PSD's/MMS under different designations (mazdoor casual labourer, contingent paid staff, daily 
wager, daily rated mazdoor, outsider) are to be treated as casual labourers. Those casual labourers who are 
engaged for a period of 8 hours a day should be described as full-time casual labourers. Those casual 
labourers who are engaged for a period of less than 8 hours a day should be described as part-time casual 
labourers. All other designations should be discontinued.” 


12. The Petitioner in the claim statement stated that the work was performed for a period of more than eight hours per 
day. The Respondent witness MW1 in his oral evidence nowhere stated that Petitioner did not perform the work 
about eight or more than 8 hours per day. 


13. The Respondent submitted another circular dated 11.09.1991 which is marked as Ex.M2. The subject of this 
circular is Casual Labourers (Grant of Temporary Status and Regularization) Scheme. This circular did not suggest 
date of appointment of the labourers which means this circular does not impose a condition that the casual labour 
must be in service on a particular date. 


14. The another circular issued by Respondent, Department of Posts, dated 27.11.1995 marked as Ex.M3, 
which suggests that full time casual labourers recruited after 29.11.1989 upto 10.09.1993 may also be considered for 
grant of benefits under the scheme. This circular later specified the particular date i.e., 10.09.1993. 


15. The next document marked as Ex.M5 dated 19.11.2010, which states that no casual labour shall be engaged 
in the administrative office with effect from 01.12.2010. This circular further stated that since the duties of waterman, 
watch & ward, gardening, cleaning etc. are now part of duties assigned to MTS, the existing practice of engaging 
casual labourers as waterman, gardener, watch and ward or any other category shall be dispensed with from 
01.12.2010. The Petitioner was engaged prior to this circular dated 19.11.2010. 


16. The next document filed by the Respondent and marked as Ex.M6 is a circular issued by Ministry of 
Communications & IT, Department of Posts dated 27.01.2011 regarding filling up of vacancies on the basis of latest 
recruitment rules for the post of MTS, wherein it was directed to observe the following conditions:- 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7109 


7) (a) 25% by appointment of Casual Labourers conferred with temporary status on the basis of Selection- 
cum-seniority failing which by, 


(b) Appointment of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 8 
hours, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(c) Appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, engaged on or before 1.9.1993, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(d) Direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time. 


, 


ii). 75% by direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time.’ 


17. This circular clearly suggests that 25% of persons must be appointed from casual labourers, who has been 
conferred with temporary status on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. The second condition suggests appointment 
of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 8 hours, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority. The third condition suggests that appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, 
engaged on or before 01.09.1993, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. 


It is true that the Respondent department never constituted any committee to select persons who conferred with 
temporary status by preparing list of selection cum seniority. 


18. All the circulars issued by Department of Posts suggest that since the Petitioner was not in service on 
01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh Vs. State of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_under:- 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, and 
they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work is 
perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly placed 
workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


19. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


7110 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 


22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the 
following directions:- 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service 
and the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits. 


The reference is answered accordingly. 
Record be consigned to the record room. 
SUSHIL KUMAR-IL Presiding Officer

5. The Petitioner has submitted proof of affidavit in support of his claim and adduced oral evidence as WW1 
and documents filed by his were marked as Ex.W1 to W17. The Respondent has also filed its proof of affidavit 
and Shri R.Swaminathan, Assistant Chief Accounts Officer was examined as MWI1 and documents on behalf of 
respondent were marked as Ex.M1 to M7. 


6. Heard the learned counsel appearing for either side and perused the records. The point that arises for 
consideration is “whether the employee of the Respondent is entitled for reinstatement into service along with all 
benefits against the management of Department of Postal Accounts & Finance? If not to what relief the concerned 
workman is entitled?” 


7. The Petitioner Shri P-Kumaran has stated in his claim statement that he had entered into service of the 
Respondent in the year 2013. The fact of continuous service is established by the Petitioner by adducing oral 
evidence as WW1 and filing proof of affidavit and the documents which were marked as Ex.W1 to W17. 


8. The Respondent in its reply admitted this fact that Petitioner was engaged with the Department, but stated 
that engagement was on daily wage basis and not against any MTS vacancies. The Petitioner was not a permanent 
employee and there was no employer-employee relationship exists between the Respondent and the Petitioner. The 
Respondent further stated that no appointment or engagement order was issued to the Petitioner and as per circular 
dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995, casual labourers in employment upto 01.09.1993 were only eligible to be 
conferred with temporary status and the Petitioner was not working on 01.09.1993 with the Department and 
therefore, they are not entitled for any absorption. 


9. The learned counsel for the Respondent further submits that Multi Tasking Staff Recruitment Rules, 2010 
dated 12.12.2010 is not applicable to the Petitioner. As per circular dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995 the following 
conditions must be fulfilled:- 


a) Temporary status on or before 01.09.1993; 
b) Full time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993 & 
c) Part-time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993. 


10. The learned counsel for the Respondent contended that Petitioner was not engaged through employment 
exchange and no appointment letter was issued. He further stated that assumption of the Petitioner that he/she works 
against the post of MTS is incorrect. The learned counsel further stated that there was no relationship of employer- 
employee between the Respondent and Petitioner, hence the question of notice or protection u/s.25F of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947 does not arise. 


11. On behalf of the Respondent a circular dated 17.05.1989 has been filed which is marked as Ex.M1, and it 
clarifies the position of casual labourers and part-time casual labourers in para 2, which reads as under:- 


“2. It is hereby clarified that all daily wagers working in Post Offices or in RMS Offices or in Administrative 
Offices or PSD's/MMS under different designations (mazdoor casual labourer, contingent paid staff, daily 
wager, daily rated mazdoor, outsider) are to be treated as casual labourers. Those casual labourers who are 
engaged for a period of & hours a day should be described as full-time casual labourers. Those casual 
labourers who are engaged for a period of less than 8 hours a day should be described as part-time casual 
labourers. All other designations should be discontinued.” 


12. The Petitioner in the claim statement stated that the work was performed for a period of more than eight hours per 
day. The Respondent witness MW1 in his oral evidence nowhere stated that Petitioner did not perform the work 
about eight or more than 8 hours per day. 


13. The Respondent submitted another circular dated 11.09.1991 which is marked as Ex.M2. The subject of this 
circular is Casual Labourers (Grant of Temporary Status and Regularization) Scheme. This circular did not suggest 
date of appointment of the labourers which means this circular does not impose a condition that the casual labour 
must be in service on a particular date. 


14. The another circular issued by Respondent, Department of Posts, dated 27.11.1995 marked as Ex.M3, 
which suggests that full time casual labourers recruited after 29.11.1989 upto 10.09.1993 may also be considered for 
grant of benefits under the scheme. This circular later specified the particular date i.e., 10.09.1993. 


15. The next document filed by the Respondent and marked as Ex.M6 is a circular issued by Ministry of 
Communications & IT, Department of Posts dated 27.01.2011 regarding filling up of vacancies on the basis of latest 
recruitment rules for the post of MTS, wherein it was directed to observe the following conditions:- 


“1) (a) 25% by appointment of Casual Labourers conferred with temporary status on the basis of Selection- 
cum-seniority failing which by, 


(b) Appointment of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 6 
hours, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


7114 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


(c) Appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, engaged on or before 1.9.1993, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(d) Direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time. 
ii). 75% by direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time.” 


16. This circular clearly suggests that 25% of persons must be appointed from casual labourers, who has been 
conferred with temporary status on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. The second condition suggests appointment 
of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 8 hours, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority. The third condition suggests that appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, 
engaged on or before 01.09.1993, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. 


It is true that the Respondent department never constituted any committee to select persons who conferred with 
temporary status by preparing list of selection cum seniority. 


17. All the circulars issued by Department of Posts suggest that since the Petitioner was not in service on 
01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh Vs. State of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_ under:- 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, and 
they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work is 
perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly placed 
workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


18. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism’”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


19. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


20. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7115 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 


21. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the 
following directions:- 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service 
and the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits. 


The reference is answered accordingly. 
Record be consigned to the record room.

AWARD 


The Central Government, Ministry of Labour& Employment vide its Order No. L-42011/360/2022-IR(DU) 
dated 12.01.2023 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“1, Whether the demands of Tamilnadu Toll Gate Employees Federation vide letter dated 12.08.2022 and Sengurichi 
Tollway Labour Progressive Federation, Ulundurpet vide letter dated 12.08.2022 against the management of National 
Highways Authority of India, Trichirapalli (Principal Employer), Trichy Tollway Private Limited, M/s SKM 
Contractor & Services Pvt. Ltd.,, M/s Lakshmi Security Services and M/s Racy Projects over their charter of demands 
regarding permanency of job under NHAI, night allowance, bonus, Increment, Medical insurance coverage etc. are 
proper, legal and justified? If yes, to what reliefs as sought vide letter under reference the disputant are entitled and 
what directors, if any, are necessary in this respect ? 


2. Whether the claim of Tamilnadu Toll Gate Employees Federation and Sengurichy Tollway Labour Progressive 
Federation, Ulundurpet that the termination of 56 workers is illegally done by the management of National Highways 
Authority of India, Trichirappalli (Principal Employer) / Trichy Tollway Private Limited / M/s SKM Contractor & 
Service Pvt. Ltd. / M/s Lakshmi Security Services / M/s Racy Projects is proper, legal and justified? If yes, to what 
relief the disputant is entitled and what directors, if any, are necessary in this respect?” 


2. On receipt of the above reference dated 12.01.2023 from the appropriate Government, the dispute was 
registered as ID No. 4/2023 and due notices were issued to both the parties for their appearance fixing the case to 
01.05.2023. Neither the Petitioner (Petition No. 1 and 2) nor any Counsel / Authorized Representative turned up 
resulting further adjournments to 26.06.2023 and 20.07.2023. The Petitioners did not turn up whereas the 27 Party 
(17, 2" and 37 Respondent filed Vakalat Nama. It reveals from the body of reference that while the appropriate Govt. 
sent the reference dated 12.01.2023 to this Tribunal for adjudication, copies of the reference were sent to the 
Petitioners and all the opposite parties. It is therefore well presumed that both parties must have received the 
reference. Even then, in the interest of justice, the Petitioners were once again directed to appear and to file claim 
statement fixing the case to 02.07.2025 and 25.08.2025. The Petitioner (Petitioner No.1 and 2) did not turn up nor was 
any authorized representative of the counsel on his behalf present. The claim statement was not furnished in any 
manner by the Petitioner (Petitioner Nol and 2). The R4 and R5 were not present, whereas R1 to R3 were present. It 
reveals the Petitioners, despite of sufficient opportunity choose not to appear or to file claim statement and 
documents. 


3. In the circumstance it deems proper not to re-list the case for the same purpose to any other date which 
would be wastage of the valuable time of this Tribunal. The case was reserved for Final Order. 


4. In view of the discussion held supra, it is crystal clear that the petitioners have got no interest to proceed with 
the case. Thus, the Tribunal is not in a position to adjudicate the dispute as referred by the Appropriate Government, 
as there exists no Industrial Dispute for adjudication as per the reference. 


5. In the result the reference is answered against the petitioners. 
An Award is passed accordingly. 
SUSHIL KUMAR-I, Presiding Officer

का.आ. 2045.---औद्योगिक विवाद अधिनियम, 1947 (1947 का 14) की धारा 17 के अनुसरण में, केन्द्रीय 
सरकार महाप्रबंधक, डाक लेखा एवं वित्त, एग्मोर; निदेशक, डाक लेखा, कार्यालय महाप्रबंधक, डाक लेखा एवं वित्त, 


7118 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


एम्मोर के प्रबंधतंत्र के संबद्ध नियोजकों और श्री पी. सेनिवासन, चेन्नई, कामगार के बीच अनुबंध में निर्दिष्ट औद्योगिक 
विवाद में केन्द्रीय सरकार औद्योगिक अधिकरण- सह- श्रम न्‍्यायालय- चेन्नई पंचाट (संदर्भ संखया- 4/2020) को जैसा कि 
अनुलग्रक में दिखाया गया है,प्रकाशित करती है।
