9. Further, domestic inquiry against CSE has been conducted strictly in accordance with the principle of natural 
justice and workman CSE has been found guilty of grave and serious acts of misconduct. Thus, finding of the inquiry 
officer is based on of oral and documentary evidence recorded during enquiry and report of inquiry officer do not 
suffers from any illegality or perversely. The inquiry officer report goes to reveal that on 1-09-2015 CSE workman, 
has committed the misconduct of physical assault to the official of Respondent Management and he has been rightly 
held guilty of committing misconduct. The details of specific acts of misconduct allegedly committed by the 
Petitioner along with other co-workman on 1-09-2015 including physical assault on Respondent staff are as follows: - 


That the Petitioner workman has physically assaulted Mr. Hari Pandu Ranga Swamy Madasu, the Chief 
Operations and Maintenance, thereby causing grievous injuries. The act not only endangered the safety of a senior 
official but also disrupted the discipline and harmony of the workplace. Further, Petitioner workman actively 
participated in a riotous mob attack, leading to the damage of company property, and creating an atmosphere of fear 
and disorder within the establishment. Such conduct undermines the safety and security of the workplace environment 
and lastly. The Petitioner workman exhibited willful insubordination by disobeying lawful and reasonable orders of 
his superiors. Furthermore, he threatened senior officials, displaying gross indiscipline and a blatant disregard for the 
hierarchical structure and decorum expected within the organization. 


10. The findings of enquiry officer are based on cogent and credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and 
documentary proof. The enquiry was conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice, providing the 
Petitioner ample opportunity to defend himself. Thus, the aforementioned acts committed by the Petitioner workman 
squarely fall under the category of serious misconduct as defined under Clauses 19(a), (c), (d) and (e) of the Andhra 
Pradesh Shops and establishments Rules, 1990. 


Rules 19 (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of AP Shops & Establishment Rules provides as here under: - 

i. Clause 19(a): Willful insubordination or disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of a superior. 
ii. Clause 19(C): Damage to the employer’s property. 

iii. Clause 19(d): Riotous or disorderly behavior in the premises of the establishment. 

iv. Clause 19(e): Threatening or intimidating any employee or superior. 


The misconduct committed by the workman along with employees of assaulting superiors, instigating others, and 
participating in the riotous violent activities constitute serious act of misconduct which strike at the root of workplace 
discipline. The act of workman causing grievous injuries to managerial staff is a grave and serious misconduct that is 
not condonable. Therefore, the dismissal order passed by Respondent against the workman is justified and 
appropriate action. 


11. Respondent has relied upon the few decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court which are relevant to the point and 
discussed as here under: - 


(a) Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishnakali Tea Estate Bharatiya Vs. Aknn Chah Mazdoor Sanah - (2004) 8 SCC 200 
upheld the dismissal of workmen who had assaulted managerial personnel causing damage to property, gherao of 
the management, wrongfully confining manager. The Apex Court observed that such violent Conduct cannot be 
taken lightly, and the punishment of dismissal was warranted to preserve discipline and safety at the workplace. 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7289 


(b) Similarly, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Muriadih Colliery Vs. Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union - 
(2005) 3 SCC 331, held that the dismissal of employees who participated in a violent mob attack, causing 
injury to the General Manager, was justified, and interference by the Labour Court under Section 11-A of the 
ID Act was disapproved and the punishment proportionate to the misconduct. was upheld. 


(c) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M.P, Electricity Board Vs. Jagdish Chandra Sharma - order (2005) 
3 SCC 401. of dismissal of a Workman who assaulted a senior officer, restored the decision of the Industrial 
Court, thereby reiterating that acts of violence by employees, particularly against their superiors, must be 
dealt with strictly and are not open to lenient treatment. The reinstatement ordered by the Labour Court was 
reversed, affirming the employer's authority to maintain discipline through dismissal. 


(d) In the case of Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka - (2006) 1 


SSC 430, the Hon’ble Supreme Court underscored the importance of workplace discipline and held that even 
provoked assault on a superior, amounts to gross indiscipline. The Court stated: "30. In view of the change in 
economic policy of the country, it may not now be proper to allow the employees to break the discipline with 
impunity. Our country is governed by the rule of law. All actions, therefore, must be taken in accordance with 
law.” 


(e) In the case of Usha Breco Mazdoor Sangh Vs. Management of M/S. Usha Breco Ltd - (2008) 5 SCC 554, 
Hon’ble Supreme Court while reaffirming the legal position laid down by it is in the case firestone Tyre and 
Rubber Co. Vs. The management and Others — (1973) 1 SCC 813, held: - 


“31. It is one thing to say that finding of an Enquiry Officer is perverse or betrays the well-known doctrine of 
proportionality another thing to say that only because two views are possible, the Labour Court shall interfere 
therewith. In other words, it is one thing to say that on the basis of the materials on record, the Labour Court comes to 
a conclusion that a verdict of guilt has been arrived at by the Enquiry Officer whereas the materials suggested 
otherwise but it is another thing to say that such a verdict was also a possible view. 


39. The upshot of our discussion is that the decision of the labour Court should not be based on mere 
hypothesis. It cannot overturn a decision of the Management on ipse dixit. Its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the 
Act although is a wide one, must be judiciously exercise either whimsically or capriciously. It may scrutinize and 
analyze the evidence but what is important is how it does so.” 


(f) Further, in the case of New Shorrock Mills vs Maheshbhai T. Rao, 1996 SCC page 590. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court held: - 


“35. In the case of New Shorrock Mills Vs. (1996) Maheshbhai T Rao 6 of SCC 590, held that: 


"Labour Court in the present case having come to a Conclusion that the finding of the departmental enquiry was legal 
and proper, the Respondents order of discharge was not by way of victimization and that the Respondent workman 
had Seriously misbehaved and was thus guilty of misconduct, ought not to have interfered with the punishment, 
which was awarded, in the manner it did. This is not a case where the Court Could Come to the conclusion that the 
punishment was awarded was shockingly disproportionate to the employee's conduct and his past service record." 


(g) The Supreme Court in the case of Northeastern Karnataka RTC Vs. Ashappa 2006 (5) SCC 137 reaffirmed 
that the Tribunal must not lightly interfere with the employer's disciplinary decisions and reiterated the "shockingly 
disproportionate" standard. 


(h) In Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka (cupra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
clarified that the days of automatic sympathy towards the workman are over, and that discipline must be maintained at 
all costs in light of contemporary industrial conditions. The Tribunal's power to substitute the employer's decision 
must be exercised with restraint. 


(i) In the case of Muriadih Colliery (Supra) & Krishnakali Tea 


Estate (Supra), the Apex Court expressly held that interference by Labour Courts with dismissal orders passed for 
acts involving violence and assault was not permissible under section 11-A of the ID Act, as the punishment was not 
disproportionate. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Honorable Apex Court as discussed above, there is ample 
oral and documentary evidence on record to substantiate the charges against the petitioner workman, and it cannot be 
said that the order of dismissal of Petitioner is perverse or shockingly disproportionate. 


12. As regard the plea of the petitioner workman that Respondent Management has victimize him due to the being 
member of the union and also for raising the demand related to welfare of the workman. 


In this context, Respondent has relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Iron 
Works versus Bhagobhai Balubhai Patel, 1976 SCC page 518. Therein Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
legal test for establishing the plea of victimization as discussed here under: - 


7290 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


"11. The onus of establishing plea of victimisation will be upon the person pleading 


it. Since a charge of victimisation is a serious matter reflecting, to a degree, subjective upon the attitude of 
the employer evidenced by acts and conduct, it has to be established by safe and sure evidence. Mere allegations, 
vague suggestions and insinuations are not enough. All particulars of the charge brought out, if believed, must be 
weighed by the Tribunal and a conclusion should be reached on a totality of the evidence produced." 


The Apex Court further held: 


"12. Once, in the opinion of the Tribunal a gross misconduct is established, as required, on legal evidence either in a 
fairly conducted domestic enquiry or before the Tribunal on merits, the plea of victimisation will not carry the case of 
the employee any further. A proved misconduct is antithesis of victimisation as understood in industrial relations." 


13. Thus, in view of the principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court, as discussed above the petitioner workman has 
failed to produce any evidence in support of the plea that the action of Respondent management in dismissing him 
from service is victimization of the petitioner workman. The petitioner workman has failed to discharge his burden of 
proof regarding plea of victimization or unfair labor practices hence same is untenable. 


14. As regard the plea of the petitioner that they he has been acquitted from the criminal trial by court in respect of 
the alleged acts of misconduct. In this context, the decision of Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Deputy 
Inspector General of Police versus Sethu . Thiruvan, 2013 SCC page 598 is relevant, wherein Honorable Apex Court 
have held that mere acquittal in a criminal trial does not nullify or override the finding of a valid domestic inquiry. 
Further, Honorable Apex Court held that the standard of proof in a criminal trial is proof beyond reasonable doubt, 
whereas in a domestic inquiry it is only preponderance of the probability. 


In the case of Commissioner of Police vs Narendra Singh, 2006 SCC page 265, Honorable Apex Court held 
that the disciplinary proceeding can proceed independently and that an employee can be dismissed from service based 
on finding of a department inquiry even if no conviction is recorded in the criminal trial. The finding in the inquiry 
against the workman is based on credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and documentary records and 
same does not warrant any interference. 


15. Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Employers Management West Bokaro Gallery Colly of TISCO Limited 
vs Concern Workman Ram Prakash Singh, 2008 LLR, page 432, 


“16. In U.P State Road Transport Corporation Vinod Kumar, 2007 (13) SCALE 690 this Court again observed that in 
the absence of a challenge to the legality or fairness of the domestic enquiry the Court should be reluctant to either 
interfere with the finding recorded by the Enquiry officer or the punishment awarded by the Punishing Authority. 


17. After going through the order of the industrial Tribunal, were are of the opinion that the Tribunal has interfered 
with the findings recorded by the domestic. Tribunal as if it was the appellate Tribunal. There was evidence present 
on record regarding indecent riotous and disorderly behavior of the Respondent towards his superiors. The 
management witness who were present at the scene of occurrence have unequivocally deposed about the misbehavior 
of the Respondent towards his superiors. Their evidence has been discarded by the Tribunals by observing that in the 
absence of independent evidence, the statements of the workmen who were present at the scene of occurrence could 
not be believed. Industrial Tribunal tell in error in discarding the evidence produce by the management only because 
the independent witnesses were not produce them. It is possible that at the time of occurrence, only the workers of the 
Management and the persons who were truing to put up the constructions dependent evidence was available. 
Statements of the fellow workmen had established the misconduct of the Respondent. Enquiry officer accepted the 
testimony of the witness produced by the management who had clearly implicated the Respondent. It was a legitimate 
conclusion which could be arrived at and it would not be open to the industrial Tribunal to substitute the said opinion 
by its own opinion. 


19. Tribunal has set aside the report of the enquiry Officer and the order of dismissal passed by the punishing 
Authority by observing that the charges against the Respondent were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. It has 
repeatedly had been held by the court that the acquittal in a criminal case could not operate as a bar for drawing up of 
a disciplinary proceeding against a delinquent. It is well settled principle of law that yardstick and standard proof in a 
criminal case is different from the one disciplinary proceeding. While the standard of proof in a criminal case is proof 
beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof in a departmental proceeding is preponderance of probabilities.” 


Further, the Honorable Supreme Court has observed that in a case where two views are possible on the 
evidence on record, then the Industrial Tribunal should be very slow in coming to a conclusion other than the one 
arrived at by the domestic Tribunal, by substituting its opinion in place of the opinion of the domestic tribunal. 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the apex court, as discussed above, the plea of the petitioner that there 
is no legal evidence on record is untenable, as there is sufficient evidence on record of the domestic inquiry to prove 
the guilt of the workman in the alleged misconduct. 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7291 


16. Further, as regard the appreciation and evaluation of the evidence in matter of domestic inquiry, Hon’ble 
Supreme Court, in the case of State of Rajasthan and others Vs Him Singh, Civil Appeal Number 3340 of 2020, 
date of decision: 29th October 2021, has laid down the principles extracted as here under: - 


“Disciplinary enquiries have to abide by the rules of natural justice. But they are not governed by strict rules of 
evidence which apply to judicial proceedings. The standard of proof is hence not the strict standard which governs a 
criminal trial, of proof be yond reasonable doubt, but a civil standard governed by a preponderance of probabilities. 
Within the rule of preponderance, there are varying approaches based on context and subject. The first end of the 
spectrum is founded on deference and autonomy -deference to the position of the disciplinary authority as a fact- 
finding authority and autonomy of the employer in maintaining discipline and efficiency of the service. Al the other 
end of the spectrum is the principle that the court has the jurisdiction to interfere when the findings in the enquiry are 
based on no evidence or when they suffer from perversity. 


To determine whether the finding in a disciplinary inquiry is based on some evidence an initial or threshold level of 
scrutiny is undertaken. That is to satisfy the conscience of the courts that there is some evidence to support the charge 
of misconduct and to guard against perversity, but this does not allow the court to re- appreciate evidentiary findings 
in a disciplinary enquiry or to substitute a view which appears lo the judge to be more appropriate. To do so would 
offend the first principle which has been outlined above. The ultimate guide is the exercise of robust common sense 
without which the judges' craft is in vain.” 


17. In the case of Hombe Gouda Education Trust Vs State of Karnataka, 2006 SCC, page 430: Hon’ble Supreme 
Court have held that assaulting a superior at a workplace amount to an act of gross indiscipline. The respondent is a 
teacher. Even under grave provocation, a teacher is not expected to abuse the head of the institution in a filthy 
language and assault him with a chappal. punishment of dismissal from service, therefore, cannot be said to be 
wholly disproportionate so as to shock one's conscience. Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that a person, when 
dismissed from service, is put to great hardship, but that would not mean that a grave misconduct (assault on superior 
at workplace) should go unpunished. Maintenance of discipline of an institution is equally important. 


18.Further, In the case of MP Electricity Board Vs Jagdish Sharma, 2005 SCC, page 401, Hon’ble Supreme Court 
have held: 


"9. In the case on hand, the employee has been found guilty of hitting and injuring his superior officer at the 
workplace obviously in the breach of Presence of other employees This clearly amounted in an discipline in the 
organisation Discipline at the workplace organisation like the employer herein, is the sine qua non for the efficient 
working of the organisation, when an employee breaches such discipline and the employer terminates his services it 
is not open to a Labour Court of an Industrial Tribunal to take view that the punishment awarded is shockingly 
disproportionate to the charge proved. We have already 


referred to the views of this Court. To quote Jack Chan, 


‘Discipline is a form of civilly responsible behaviour which helps maintain social order and contributes to 
the preservation, if not advancement, of collective interests of society at large.’ 


Obviously, this idea is more relevant in considering the working of an organisation like the employer herein or an 
industrial undertaking. Obedience to authority in a workplace is not slavery. It is rot violative of one's natural rights. It 
is essential for the prosperity of the organisation as well as that of its employee’s. When in such a situation, a 
punishment of termination is awarded for hitting and injuring a superior officer supervising the work of the employee, 
with no extenuating circumstance established, it cannot be said to be not justified. It cannot certainly be termed 
unduly harsh or disproportionate. The Labour Court and the High Court in this case totally misdirected themselves 
while exercising their jurisdiction. The Industrial Court made the correct approach and came to the right conclusion." 


19. Further, in the case of Ajit Kumar Nag Vs Indian Oil Corporation Limited, 2005 SCC page 764, the 
Honorable Supreme Court has held, in a three-judge bench, in paragraph 56, "It is well settled that the burden of 
proving malafide is on the person making the allegation, and the burden is very heavy. There is every presumption in 
favor of the administration that the power has been exercised bona fide and in good faith. It is to be remembered that 
the allegations of malafide are often more easily made than made out, and the very seriousness of such allegations 
demands proof of a high degree of credibility." 


Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that assault, intimidation are penal offences. A workman indulging in 
commission of criminal offenses should not be spared only because he happens to be a union leader. The act does not 
encourage indiscipline. It will be a matter of some concern if the opinion of the inquiry officer can be totally ignored, 
despite the fact that the management is precluded from adducing any fresh evidence before the labor court. A union 
leader does not enjoy immunity from being proceeded with in a case of misconduct. 


20. का the case of D. Mulchandani Electric and Radio Industries Limited Vs Workman, 1975 Supreme Court Cases 
page 731, Hon’ble Supreme Court have held: 


establishment 


7292 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


“Tt was not disputed before us that the allegation of assault, if proved, would be an act subversive of discipline: what 
was contended on behalf of the respondent was between Thana and the premises was that the alleged assault having 
taken place in the train Mulund which was obviously outside the or precincts of the establishment, was not covered by 
Standing Order. 


24(1). The Labour Court also found that the alleged assault did not In our amount to misconduct under Standing 
Order 24(1) which, it was held was restricted to acts and omissions inside the premises of the establish opinion, Lon a 
plain reading of the clause, the words "within the premises or precincts of the establishment" refer not to the place 
where the act which is subversive of discipline or good behaviour is committed but where the consequence of such an 
act manifests itself. In other words, an act, wherever committed, if it has the effect of sub- verting discipline or good 
behaviour within the premises or precincts of the establishment, will amount to misconduct under Standing Order 
24(1) We are unable to agree that Standing Order 24(1) leaves out of its scone an act committed outside though it may 
result in subversion of discipline or good behaviour within the premises or precincts of the establishment in question. 
Such a construction in our view would be quite unreasonable.” 


21. In the case of State bank of Bikaner and Jaipur vs Nemi Channel via 2011 Supreme Court cases page 580 
Hon’ble Supreme Court have held that subsequent acquittal by criminal court will not in any way render completed 
discipline proceeding invalid, nor affect the validity of finding of the guilt and consequential punishment. 


22. Thus, in view of the foregone discussion and law laid down by the apex court as discussed above, in the instant 
matter all the charges framed and proved in domestic inquiry against the workman being serious and grave in nature 
and stands proved by oral and documentary evidence recorded and produced bin the inquiry. Further, the evidence 
produced by the management before inquiry is legal and admissible as per principle of preponderance of probability 
laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court in its various decisions as discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award. 
Therefore, order of dismissal of Petitioner workman cannot be faulted with, nor it can be said to be in any way 
disproportionate to the gravity of the charges. Thus, the punishment of dismissal of the workman is proportionate to 
the gravity of the charges, and hence deserve to be upheld. Thus, the action of the respondent management in 
dismissing the services of the workman is held legal and justified. 


This issue is decided against the workman and in favor of the respondent management. 
Issue No: IV 


In view of foregone discussion and finding given at issue No. I, II and III, I am of the considered opinion 
that the action of Respondent management in dismissing the Petitioner from service vide order dated 30-08-2016 is 
legal and justified. Therefore, no interference warrants in the punishment of dismissal order dated 30-08-2016 of the 
Petitioner and the action of Respondent Management is held legal and justified and liable to be confirmed. 


This Issue is decided accordingly. 
AWARD 


In view of the foregone discussion and finding given at issue No. I, II, III, and IV, the action of 
Respondent Management in dismissing the service of the Petitioner workman vide order dated 30-08-2016 is held 
legal and justified. Petition filed by the Petitioner sans merit hence dismissed. 


Award passed accordingly. Transmit.

1. This Petition has been filed by the Petitioner workman under section 2(A) (2) of Industrial Dispute Act 1947 
with the prayer to set aside his dismissal order dated 277 May 2016 passed by the Respondent Management and to direct 
the Respondent to reinstate Petitioner in the service with continuity of service with all back wages and all other attendant 
benefits. 


2. The facts in brief culled out from the petition are that the Petitioner workman was appointed as a Toll Collector 
in Swarna Tollway Private Limited Organization on 23" June 2004. 


Further, Petitioner submitted that he was place under suspension with issuing Charge sheet on 97 September 
2015, and without considering his explanation Respondent has dismissed him vide order dated 27" May 2016. Further, 
Petitioner submitted that on 11 September 2015 he was member of Swarna Toll Employees Union, and he went to 
Budanam Base Camp office to meet with office bearer of the union and number of employees, union president and some 
other office bearers were also present at Budanam base camp office to meet with the COM to represent their demands. 
When the union leader entered into the Chamber of COM. Other employees were waiting outside camp office of COM 
and Some discussions took place between Union leaders and the management. As per petitioner COM did not consider 
the lawful demands of the employees and union leaders came outside and explained to other employees. Since lawful 
demands were not considered by the Respondent COM, Union leaders and employees expressed their protest against the 
Respondent Management by shouting slogans. COM and other managers foisted a false case against the petitioner and rest 
of the employees present there at Chillakuru Police Station. The Police authority registered a case in Crime No.154/2015 
against the 28 employees and they sent the there employees to remand. The Chief of operation and maintenance and other 
Toll Managers made a complaint what has been alleged in the charge sheet. Further, Petitioner stated that he was no way 
concerned in the said incident there was no specific allegation against him. The allegations made against all the 28 
employees are in common Petitioner contended that before issuing charge sheet, the copy of complaint was not supplied to 
him to submit his explanation and he never committed any misconduct of willful in subordination or disobedience with the 
lawful and reasonable order of superior. He never damage the employer’s business or property and did not instigate co- 
workman to misbehave with official of Management. He never committed any act subversive of discipline and I never 
assaulted and grievously hurting the management as alleged in the charge sheet. Further, Petitioner submitted that enquiry 
has been conducted by the enquiry officer into the allegations without following principle of natural justice. There was no 
corroborative evidence to prove the guilt of Petitioner and only management witness were examined in the enquiry. The 
management witness nowhere has stated that what acts, and omission committed by C.S.E and, there was no legal 
evidence to prove the allegations against C.S.E. Thus, enquiry officer has also failed to bring home the guilt of C.S.E and 
gave common findings of all the 28 C.S.E which is not legal. Enquiry officer has conducted enquiry an empty formality, 
and submitted his report holding that the allegation are proved. The procedure followed by the enquiry office, and enquiry 
findings are not fair, proper and not maintainable under law. Respondent management had issued show cause notice to 
petitioner and without considering his explanation the Respondent management passed his dismissal order on 27-05-2016 
that is not sustainable under law. 


Further, Petitioner submitted that the allegation leveled against him were false and fabricated and there was no 
specific allegation against him for violation of any acts or omissions. All the common allegations has been made against 
the 28 employees. There was no willful in subordination or disobedience of instruction in connection with the order of the 
superior and no damages done with the employer business or property. There was no unprovoked behavior with customers 
riotous disorderly or indecent behavior in premises of the establishment. There was no act subversive of discipline. It is 
submitted that Petitioner had not committed due serious misconduct to dismiss him from service. Further it is submitted 
that Petitioner filed the ID No 14 of 2017 before the labour Court Guntur and labour court passed the order dated 31 -8- 
2019 thereby rejecting the petition on the ground of lack jurisdiction. Therefore, any delay in filing the appeal is on 
account of COVID-19 pandemic situations prevailing all over the world. Therefore, prayed to set aside the order dated 27- 
05-2016 passed by Respondent and to reinstate the Petitioner in the service,

4. On the basis of submission of either parties, following issues arise for determination in the present matter: - 
1. Whether the departmental enquiry held against the Petitioner is legal and valid? 


2. Whether present petition filed by Petitioner raising industrial Dispute against his dismissal order 30-08- 
2016 is barred by limitation? 


3. Whether action of Respondent management Director, Swarna Toll way private Limited, Hyderabad, vide 
order dated 27-05-2016 whereby in terminating the services of the Petitioner is legal and justified? 


4. To what relief If any, Petitioner, is entitled for? 
Findings: - 
Issue No. I 


The Departmental inquiry conducted against the Workman Sri. Daggu Sathish has been held legal and valid, by 
this court vide order dated 11" November 2024. 


Thus, issue is decided accordingly. 
Issue No. II 


In this context, Respondent No.2 and 3 contended that the present Industrial Dispute has been raised by the Petitioner 
on 2™ August 2021 after the lapse of five years from the date of his dismissal order dated 27" May 2016. Therefore, in 
view of the provision contained under section 2-A (3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, this claim could be filed by the 
Petitioner before the expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment, or otherwise termination of 
service as specified in (1) of section 2-A. Therefore, the present claim Petition raising the Industrial Dispute by Petitioner 
under section 2A (2) of the ID Act, is barred by limitation. 


The perusal of claim petition goes to reveals that Petitioner has raised the Industrial Dispute against his dismissal order, 
dated 30" august 2016 passed the by the Respondent Management by filing claim petition in the year 2021. In the para 11 
of claim petition, Petitioner has averred that against his termination order, he approached to the Deputy Labour 
Commissioner of Labor, Nellore for cancellation and same was dismissed without considering the merit. Thereafter, he 
filed petition before Labour court, Guntur, which got registered as ID Number 201/2016. Labour Court, Guntur, vide 
order dated 31“ August 2019, has returned his petition on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. Thereafter due to COVID-19 
pandemic situation Petitioner could not approach this court within time. Petitioner has also filed the copy of the order 
dated 31-08-2019 passed by the Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Guntur, in ID no. 201/2016, whereby Labour Court 
Guntur has returned petition of the Petitioner for presentation before the appropriate court of jurisdiction. It is established 
fact that in the year 2020, there was a prevailing situation of COVID-19 pandemic and Petitioner was not able to approach 
this court to present petition at Hyderabad. Thus, Petitioner has furnished cogent and sufficient explanation of delay in 
filing the present petition and same is not fatal to present Industrial Dispute. Therefore, in view of the above present 
petition raising the Industrial Dispute under section 2-A (2) of the ID Act, against the dismissal order dated 30-08-2016 is 
not barred by limitation. Issue is decided in favor of the Petitioner. 


Issue No. III 


The perusal of record goes to reveal that in this claim petition, petitioner has challenged his dismissal order dated 
27" May 2016 passed by Respondent Management on the grounds alleged in petition. Furthermore, perusal of the record 
of inquiry proceeding along with inquiry report, goes to reveal that the Petitioner was given fair opportunity of hearing at 
every stage of proceedings, which he availed, without raising any objection complaining of any prejudice of any nature 
caused to him before the inquiry officer at any point of time. Further, it is noticed that the Workman CSC received all the 
documents filed and relied upon by the Respondent management in support of the charge sheet, and CSC workman also 
filed a reply, cross-examined the management witnesses, and also examined himself as a witness in defense. Thus, the 
workman CSC has participated in the inquiry proceeding at every stage. Inquiry officer, on appreciation of evidence 
recorded in inquiry has submitted his reasoned report holding the workman guilty of the charges. Therefore, in the opinion 
of the court, no case is made out to hold that the domestic inquiry suffers from any procedural lapses or was conducted in 
violation of principles of natural justice, thereby causing any prejudice to the rights of the Petitioner. Moreover, validity 
and legality of the domestic inquiry has been upheld by the court vide order dated 117 November 2024. Thus, the plea of 
the Petitioner that the domestic inquiry was conducted against the Petitioner in violation of principle of natural justice is 
untenable. 


It is settled law that once it is held that the domestic inquiry is legal and proper, the next question arises for 
consideration whether the punishment imposed on the Petitioner is just and legal, or it is disproportionate to the gravity of 
the charges. Petitioner has challenged his dismissal order on the ground that the allegations leveled against him are false 
and fabricated, and during the inquiry no other employee as witness was examined to prove the charges and there was no 
corroborating evidence to prove the guilt and only that management witness were examined in the inquiry. Further, it is 
contended that there was no legal evidence before enquiry to prove the allegations, and the inquiry officer had also failed 
to bring home the charge against the Petitioner. Further, Petitioner has strenuously argued that the inquiry officer 


7298 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


conducted the inquiry as empty formality and without having any valid and legal evidence and came to the conclusion that 
allegations are proved. Further, it is urged Petitioner that had not committed any misconduct as alleged in the charge sheet, 
and there was no evidence of loss of revenue to the corporation. Further, it is contended that there was no willful 
insubordination or disobedience of instructions in connection with the orders of the superior. There was no damage or 
dishonesty in connection with the employer’s business or property, and Petitioner was not involved in unprovoked 
misbehavior with the customer, riotous, disorderly, or indecent behavior in the premises of the establishment. Lastly it is 
pleaded that the dismissal order passed by the Respondent management is grossly disproportionate to the gravity of the 
offense, and same is liable to be set aside. In view of plea taken by Petitioner, peruse the record of inquiry proceeding. 


5. The record of proceeding goes to reveal that charge sheet dated 9" September 2015 was furnished to CSE Workman 
and inquiry was conducted by the inquiry officer, in the presence of CSC workman, as well as his defense representative 
and management witness were examined during the inquiry proceedings. In support of Charge sheet against the CSC 
workman, Respondent management has examined as many as ten witnesses namely, Mr. Subramanyam Vijay deepak 
(MW1), Mr. Hari pandarunga Swami MW2, Mr. Vikram Simha Reddy MW3, Mr. R.V. Prasad (MW4), Mr. 1. Krishna 
Kishore (MWS), Mr. Vijay Kumar (MW6), Mr. L. Elvis Lionel (MW7), Mr. K.V. Ramprasad (MW$8), and Mr. 8. Vijay 
Sarathi Babu (MW9), and lastly, Mr. D. Veera swami (MW10). All the above stated witnesses, in their deposition have 
substantiated the allegations of the charge sheet issued against the CSC workman. The charge Sheet contains the 
allegation against CSE workman extracted as here under:

11. Further, domestic inquiry against CSE has been conducted strictly in accordance with the principle of natural 
justice and workman CSE has been found guilty of grave and serious acts of misconduct. Thus, finding of the inquiry 
officer is based on of oral and documentary evidence recorded during enquiry and report of inquiry officer do not suffers 
from any illegality or perversely. The inquiry officer report goes to reveal that on 1-09-2015 CSE workman, has 
committed the misconduct of physical assault to the official of Respondent Management and he has been rightly held 
guilty of committing misconduct. The details of specific acts of misconduct allegedly committed by the Petitioner along 
with other co-workman on 1-09-2015 including physical assault on Respondent staff are as follows: - 


That the Petitioner workman has physically assaulted Mr. Hari Pandu Ranga Swamy Madasu, the Chief 
Operations and Maintenance, thereby causing grievous injuries. The act not only endangered the safety of a senior official 
but also disrupted the discipline and harmony of the workplace. Further, Petitioner workman actively participated in a 
riotous mob attack, leading to the damage of company property, and creating an atmosphere of fear and disorder within 
the establishment. Such conduct undermines the safety and security of the workplace environment and lastly. The 
Petitioner workman exhibited willful insubordination by disobeying lawful and reasonable orders of his superiors. 
Furthermore, he threatened senior officials, displaying gross indiscipline and a blatant disregard for the hierarchical 
structure and decorum expected within the organization. 


12. The findings of enquiry officer are based on cogent and credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and 
documentary proof. The enquiry was conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice, providing the 
Petitioner ample opportunity to defend himself. Thus, the aforementioned acts committed by the Petitioner workman 
squarely fall under the category of serious misconduct as defined under Clauses 19(a), (c), (d) and (e) of the Andhra 
Pradesh Shops and establishments Rules, 1990. 


Rules 19 (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of AP Shops & Establishment Rules provides as here under: - 

i. Clause 19(a): Willful insubordination or disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of a superior. 
ii. Clause 19(C): Damage to the employer’s property. 

iii. Clause 19(d): Riotous or disorderly behavior in the premises of the establishment. 

iv. Clause 19(e): Threatening or intimidating any employee or superior. 


The misconduct committed by the workman along with employees of assaulting superiors, instigating others, and 
participating in the riotous violent activities constitute serious act of misconduct which strike at the root of workplace 
discipline. The act of workman causing grievous injuries to managerial staff is a grave and serious misconduct that is not 
condonable. Therefore, the dismissal order passed by Respondent against the workman is justified and appropriate action.

13. Respondent has relied upon the few decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court which are relevant to the point and discussed 
as here under: - 


(a) Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishnakali Tea Estate Bharatiya Vs. Aknn Chah Mazdoor Sanah - (2004) 8 SCC 200 
upheld the dismissal of workmen who had assaulted managerial personnel causing damage to property, gherao of the 
management, wrongfully confining manager. The Apex Court observed that such violent Conduct cannot be taken 
lightly, and the punishment of dismissal was warranted to preserve discipline and safety at the workplace. 


(b) Similarly, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Muriadih Colliery Vs. Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union - (2005) 3 
SCC 331, held that the dismissal of employees who participated in a violent mob attack, causing injury to the 
General Manager, was justified, and interference by the Labour Court under Section 11-A of the ID Act was 
disapproved and the punishment proportionate to the misconduct. was upheld. 


(c) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M.P, Electricity Board Vs. Jagdish Chandra Sharma - order (2005) 3 
SCC 4o1. of dismissal of a Workman who assaulted a senior officer, restored the decision of the Industrial Court, 
thereby reiterating that acts of violence by employees, particularly against their superiors, must be dealt with 
strictly and are not open to lenient treatment. The reinstatement ordered by the Labour Court was reversed, 
affirming the employer's authority to maintain discipline through dismissal. 


(d) In the case of Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka - (2006) 1 


SSC 430, the Hon’ble Supreme Court underscored the importance of workplace discipline and held that even 
provoked assault on a superior, amounts to gross indiscipline. The Court stated: "30. In view of the change in 
economic policy of the country, it may not now be proper to allow the employees to break the discipline with 
impunity. Our country is governed by the rule of law. All actions, therefore, must be taken in accordance with law.” 


(e) Inthe case of Usha Breco Mazdoor Sangh Vs. Management of M/S. Usha Breco Ltd — (2008) 5 SCC 554, Hon’ble 
Supreme Court while reaffirming the legal position laid down by it is in the case firestone Tyre and Rubber Co. Vs. 
The management and Others — (1973) 1 SCC 813, held: - 


“31. It is one thing to say that finding of an Enquiry Officer is perverse or betrays the well-known doctrine of 
proportionality another thing to say that only because two views are possible, the Labour Court shall interfere therewith. 
In other words, it is one thing to say that on the basis of the materials on record, the Labour Court comes to a conclusion 
that a verdict of guilt has been arrived at by the Enquiry Officer whereas the materials suggested otherwise but it is 
another thing to say that such a verdict was also a possible view. 


39. The upshot of our discussion is that the decision of the labour Court should not be based on mere hypothesis. 
It cannot overturn a decision of the Management on ipse dixit. Its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the Act although is a 
wide one, must be judiciously exercise either whimsically or capriciously. It may scrutinize and analyze the evidence but 
what is important is how it does so.” 


(f) Further, in the case of New Shorrock Mills vs Maheshbhai T. Rao, 1996 SCC page 590. Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held: - 


“35. In the case of New Shorrock Mills Vs. (1996) Maheshbhai T Rao 6 of SCC 590, held that: 


"Labour Court in the present case having come to a Conclusion that the finding of the departmental enquiry was legal and 
proper, the Respondents order of discharge was not by way of victimization and that the Respondent workman had 
Seriously misbehaved and was thus guilty of misconduct, ought not to have interfered with the punishment, which was 
awarded, in the manner it did. This is not a case where the Court Could Come to the conclusion that the punishment was 
awarded was shockingly disproportionate to the employee's conduct and his past service record." 


(g) The Supreme Court in the case of Northeastern Karnataka RTC Vs. Ashappa 2006 (5) SCC 137 reaffirmed that 
the Tribunal must not lightly interfere with the employer's disciplinary decisions and reiterated the "shockingly 
disproportionate” standard. 


(h) In Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka (cupra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court clarified that the 
days of automatic sympathy towards the workman are over, and that discipline must be maintained at all costs in light of 
contemporary industrial conditions. The Tribunal's power to substitute the employer's decision must be exercised with 
restraint. 


(i) In the case of Muriadih Colliery (Supra) & Krishnakali Tea 


Estate (Supra), the Apex Court expressly held that interference by Labour Courts with dismissal orders passed for acts 
involving violence and assault was not permissible under section 11-A of the ID Act, as the punishment was not 
disproportionate. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Honorable Apex Court as discussed above, there is ample oral 
and documentary evidence on record to substantiate the charges against the petitioner workman, and it cannot be said that 
the order of dismissal of Petitioner is perverse or shockingly disproportionate.

14. As regard the plea of the petitioner workman that Respondent Management has victimize him due to the being 
member of the union and also for raising the demand related to welfare of the workman. 


In this context, Respondent has relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Iron Works 
versus Bhagobhai Balubhai Patel, 1976 SCC page 518. Therein Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the legal test for 
establishing the plea of victimization as discussed here under: - 


"11. The onus of establishing plea of victimisation will be upon the person pleading 


it. Since a charge of victimisation is a serious matter reflecting, to a degree, subjective upon the attitude of the 
employer evidenced by acts and conduct, it has to be established by safe and sure evidence. Mere allegations, vague 
suggestions and insinuations are not enough. All particulars of the charge brought out, if believed, must be weighed by the 
Tribunal and a conclusion should be reached on a totality of the evidence produced." 


The Apex Court further held: 


"12. Once, in the opinion of the Tribunal a gross misconduct is established, as required, on legal evidence either in a fairly 
conducted domestic enquiry or before the Tribunal on merits, the plea of victimisation will not carry the case of the 
employee any further. A proved misconduct is antithesis of victimisation as understood in industrial relations." 


15. Thus, in view of the principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court, as discussed above the petitioner workman has 
failed to produce any evidence in support of the plea that the action of Respondent management in dismissing him from 
service is victimization of the petitioner workman. The petitioner workman has failed to discharge his burden of proof 
regarding plea of victimization or unfair labor practices hence same is untenable. 


16. As regard the plea of the petitioner that they he has been acquitted from the criminal trial by court in respect of the 
alleged acts of misconduct. In this context, the decision of Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Deputy Inspector 
General of Police versus Sethu . Thiruvan, 2013 SCC page 598 is relevant, wherein Honorable Apex Court have held that 
mere acquittal in a criminal trial does not nullify or override the finding of a valid domestic inquiry. Further, Honorable 
Apex Court held that the standard of proof in a criminal trial is proof beyond reasonable doubt, whereas in a domestic 
inquiry it is only preponderance of the probability. 


In the case of Commissioner of Police vs Narendra Singh, 2006 SCC page 265, Honorable Apex Court held that 
the disciplinary proceeding can proceed independently and that an employee can be dismissed from service based on 
finding of a department inquiry even if no conviction is recorded in the criminal trial. The finding in the inquiry against 
the workman is based on credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and documentary records and same does not 
warrant any interference. 


17. Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Employers Management West Bokaro Gallery Colly of TISCO Limited vs 
Concern Workman Ram Prakash Singh, 2008 LLR, page 432, 


“16. In U.P State Road Transport Corporation Vinod Kumar, 2007 (13) SCALE 690 this Court again observed that in the 
absence of a challenge to the legality or fairness of the domestic enquiry the Court should be reluctant to either interfere 
with the finding recorded by the Enquiry officer or the punishment awarded by the Punishing Authority. 


17. After going through the order of the industrial Tribunal, were are of the opinion that the Tribunal has interfered with 
the findings recorded by the domestic. Tribunal as if it was the appellate Tribunal. There was evidence present on record 
regarding indecent riotous and disorderly behavior of the Respondent towards his superiors. The management witness who 
were present at the scene of occurrence have unequivocally deposed about the misbehavior of the Respondent towards his 
superiors. Their evidence has been discarded by the Tribunals by observing that in the absence of independent evidence, 
the statements of the workmen who were present at the scene of occurrence could not be believed. Industrial Tribunal tell 
in error in discarding the evidence produce by the management only because the independent witnesses were not produce 
them. It is possible that at the time of occurrence, only the workers of the Management and the persons who were truing to 
put up the constructions dependent evidence was available. Statements of the fellow workmen had established the 
misconduct of the Respondent. Enquiry officer accepted the testimony of the witness produced by the management who 
had clearly implicated the Respondent. It was a legitimate conclusion which could be arrived at and it would not be open 
to the industrial Tribunal to substitute the said opinion by its own opinion. 


19. Tribunal has set aside the report of the enquiry Officer and the order of dismissal passed by the punishing Authority by 
observing that the charges against the Respondent were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. It has repeatedly had been 
held by the court that the acquittal in a criminal case could not operate as a bar for drawing up of a disciplinary proceeding 
against a delinquent. It is well settled principle of law that yardstick and standard proof in a criminal case is different from 
the one disciplinary proceeding. While the standard of proof in a criminal case is proof beyond all reasonable doubt, the 
standard of proof in a departmental proceeding is preponderance of probabilities.” 


Further, the Honorable Supreme Court has observed that in a case where two views are possible on the evidence 
on record, then the Industrial Tribunal should be very slow in coming to a conclusion other than the one arrived at by the 
domestic Tribunal, by substituting its opinion in place of the opinion of the domestic tribunal. 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7303 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the apex court, as discussed above, the plea of the petitioner that there is no 
legal evidence on record is untenable, as there is sufficient evidence on record of the domestic inquiry to prove the guilt of 
the workman in the alleged misconduct. 


18. Further, as regard the appreciation and evaluation of the evidence in matter of domestic inquiry, Hon’ble Supreme 
Court, in the case of State of Rajasthan and others Vs Him Singh, Civil Appeal Number 3340 of 2020, date of 
decision: 29th October 2021, has laid down the principles extracted as here under: - 


“Disciplinary enquiries have to abide by the rules of natural justice. But they are not governed by strict rules of evidence 
which apply to judicial proceedings. The standard of proof is hence not the strict standard which governs a criminal trial, 
of proof be yond reasonable doubt, but a civil standard governed by a preponderance of probabilities. Within the rule of 
preponderance, there are varying approaches based on context and subject. The first end of the spectrum is founded on 
deference and autonomy -deference to the position of the disciplinary authority as a fact-finding authority and autonomy 
of the employer in maintaining discipline and efficiency of the service. Al the other end of the spectrum is the principle 
that the court has the jurisdiction to interfere when the findings in the enquiry are based on no evidence or when they 
suffer from perversity. 


To determine whether the finding in a disciplinary inquiry is based on some evidence an initial or threshold level of 
scrutiny is undertaken. That is to satisfy the conscience of the courts that there is some evidence to support the charge of 
misconduct and to guard against perversity, but this does not allow the court to re- appreciate evidentiary findings in a 
disciplinary enquiry or to substitute a view which appears lo the judge to be more appropriate. To do so would offend the 
first principle which has been outlined above. The ultimate guide is the exercise of robust common sense without which 
the judges' craft is in vain.” 


19. In the case of Hombe Gouda Education Trust Vs State of Karnataka, 2006 SCC, page 430: Hon’ble Supreme Court 
have held that assaulting a superior at a workplace amount to an act of gross indiscipline. The respondent is a teacher. 
Even under grave provocation, a teacher is not expected to abuse the head of the institution in a filthy language and assault 
him with a chappal. punishment of dismissal from service, therefore, cannot be said to be wholly disproportionate so as to 
shock one's conscience. Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that a person, when dismissed from service, is put to great 
hardship, but that would not mean that a grave misconduct (assault on superior at workplace) should go unpunished. 
Maintenance of discipline of an institution is equally important. 


20.Further, In the case of MP Electricity Board Vs Jagdish Sharma, 2005 SCC, page 401, Hon’ble Supreme Court have 
held: 


"9. In the case on hand, the employee has been found guilty of hitting and injuring his superior officer at the workplace 
obviously in the breach of Presence of other employees This clearly amounted in an discipline in the organisation 
Discipline at the workplace organisation like the employer herein, is the sine qua non for the efficient working of the 
organisation, when an employee breaches such discipline and the employer terminates his services it is not open to a 
Labour Court of an Industrial Tribunal to take view that the punishment awarded is shockingly disproportionate to the 
charge proved. We have already 


referred to the views of this Court. To quote Jack Chan, 


‘Discipline is a form of civilly responsible behaviour which helps maintain social order and contributes to the 
preservation, if not advancement, of collective interests of society at large.’ 


Obviously, this idea is more relevant in considering the working of an organisation like the employer herein or an 
industrial undertaking. Obedience to authority in a workplace is not slavery. It is rot violative of one's natural rights. It is 
essential for the prosperity of the organisation as well as that of its employee’s. When in such a situation, a punishment of 
termination is awarded for hitting and injuring a superior officer supervising the work of the employee, with no 
extenuating circumstance established, it cannot be said to be not justified. It cannot certainly be termed unduly harsh or 
disproportionate. The Labour Court and the High Court in this case totally misdirected themselves while exercising their 
jurisdiction. The Industrial Court made the correct approach and came to the right conclusion." 


21. Further, in the case of Ajit Kumar Nag Vs Indian Oil Corporation Limited, 2005 SCC page 764, the Honorable 
Supreme Court has held, in a three-judge bench, in paragraph 56, "It is well settled that the burden of proving 
malafide is on the person making the allegation, and the burden is very heavy. There is every presumption in favor of the 
administration that the power has been exercised bona fide and in good faith. It is to be remembered that the allegations of 
malafide are often more easily made than made out, and the very seriousness of such allegations demands proof of a high 
degree of credibility." 


Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that assault, intimidation are penal offences. A workman indulging in 
commission of criminal offenses should not be spared only because he happens to be a union leader. The act does not 
encourage indiscipline. It will be a matter of some concern if the opinion of the inquiry officer can be totally ignored, 
despite the fact that the management is precluded from adducing any fresh evidence before the labor court. A union leader 
does not enjoy immunity from being proceeded with in a case of misconduct.

22. In the case of D. Mulchandani Electric and Radio Industries Limited Vs Workman, 1975 Supreme Court Cases page 
731, Hon’ble Supreme Court have held: 


establishment 


“Tt was not disputed before us that the allegation of assault, if proved, would be an act subversive of discipline: what was 
contended on behalf of the respondent was between Thana and the premises was that the alleged assault having taken 
place in the train Mulund which was obviously outside the or precincts of the establishment, was not covered by Standing 
Order. 


24(1). The Labour Court also found that the alleged assault did not In our amount to misconduct under Standing Order 
24(1) which, it was held was restricted to acts and omissions inside the premises of the establish opinion, Lon a plain 
reading of the clause, the words "within the premises or precincts of the establishment" refer not to the place where the act 
which is subversive of discipline or good behaviour is committed but where the consequence of such an act manifests 
itself. In other words, an act, wherever committed, if it has the effect of sub- verting discipline or good behaviour within 
the premises or precincts of the establishment, will amount to misconduct under Standing Order 24(1) We are unable to 
agree that Standing Order 24(1) leaves out of its scone an act committed outside though it may result in subversion of 
discipline or good behaviour within the premises or precincts of the establishment in question. Such a construction in our 
view would be quite unreasonable.” 


23. In the case of State bank of Bikaner and Jaipur vs Nemi Channel via 2011 Supreme Court cases page 580 
Hon’ble Supreme Court have held that subsequent acquittal by criminal court will not in any way render completed 
discipline proceeding invalid, nor affect the validity of finding of the guilt and consequential punishment. 


24. Thus, in view of the foregone discussion and law laid down by the apex court as discussed above, in the instant 
matter all the charges framed and proved in domestic inquiry against the workman being serious and grave in nature and 
stands proved by oral and documentary evidence recorded and produced bin the inquiry. Further, the evidence produced 
by the management before inquiry is legal and admissible as per principle of preponderance of probability laid down by 
Hon’ble Supreme Court in its various decisions as discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award. Therefore, order of 
dismissal of Petitioner workman cannot be faulted with, nor it can be said to be in any way disproportionate to the gravity 
of the charges. Thus, the punishment of dismissal of the workman is proportionate to the gravity of the charges, and hence 
deserve to be upheld. Thus, the action of the respondent management in dismissing the services of the workman is held 
legal and justified. 


This issue is decided against the workman and in favor of the respondent management. 
Issue No: IV 


In view of foregone discussion and finding given at issue No. I, II and III, I am of the considered opinion that the action 
of Respondent management in dismissing the Petitioner from service vide order dated 27-05-2016 is legal and justified. 
Therefore, no interference warrants in the punishment of dismissal order dated 27-05-2016 of the Petitioner and the 
action of Respondent Management is held legal and justified and liable to be confirmed. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregone discussion and finding given at issue No. 1, II, HI, and IV, the action of Respondent 
Management in dismissing the service of the Petitioner workman vide order dated 27-05-2016 is held legal and justified. 
Petition filed by the Petitioner sans merit hence dismissed.

[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7309 


Heard the argument of learned counsel for petitioner as well as Respondent. Both the parties have also filed 
their written submission. Pursue the record. 


4. On the basis of submission of either parties, following issues arise for determination in the present matter: - 
1. Whether the departmental enquiry held against the Petitioner is legal and valid? 


2. Whether present petition filed by Petitioner raising industrial Dispute against his dismissal order 30- 
08-2016 is barred by limitation? 


3. Whether action of Respondent management Director, Swarna Toll way private Limited, Hyderabad, 
vide order dated 27-05-2016 whereby in terminating the services of the Petitioner is legal and 
justified? 


4. To what relief If any, Petitioner, is entitled for? 
Findings: - 
Issue No. I 


The Departmental inquiry conducted against the Workman Sri. Daggu Sathish has been held legal and valid, 
by this court vide order dated 117 November 2024. 


Thus, issue is decided accordingly. 
Issue No. II 


In this context, Respondent No.2 and 3 contended that the present Industrial Dispute has been raised by the 
Petitioner on 2" August 2021 after the lapse of five years from the date of his dismissal order dated 27" May 2016. 
Therefore, in view of the provision contained under section 2-A (3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, this claim could be 
filed by the Petitioner before the expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment, or 
otherwise termination of service as specified in (1) of section 2-A. Therefore, the present claim Petition raising the 
Industrial Dispute by Petitioner under section 2A (2) of the ID Act, is barred by limitation. 


The perusal of claim petition goes to reveals that Petitioner has raised the Industrial Dispute against his dismissal 
order, dated 30" august 2016 passed the by the Respondent Management by filing claim petition in the year 2021. In 
the para 11 of claim petition, Petitioner has averred that against his termination order, he approached to the Deputy 
Labour Commissioner of Labor, Nellore for cancellation and same was dismissed without considering the merit. 
Thereafter, he filed petition before Labour court, Guntur, which got registered as ID Number 206/2016. Labour 
Court, Guntur, vide order dated 317 August 2019, has returned his petition on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. 
Thereafter due to COVID-19 pandemic situation Petitioner could not approach this court within time. Petitioner has 
also filed the copy of the order dated 31-08-2019 passed by the Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Guntur, in ID no. 
206/2016, whereby Labour Court Guntur has returned petition of the Petitioner for presentation before the appropriate 
court of jurisdiction. It is established fact that in the year 2020, there was a prevailing situation of COVID-19 
pandemic and Petitioner was not able to approach this court to present petition at Hyderabad. Thus, Petitioner has 
furnished cogent and sufficient explanation of delay in filing the present petition and same is not fatal to present 
Industrial Dispute. Therefore, in view of the above present petition raising the Industrial Dispute under section 2-A 
(2) of the ID Act, against the dismissal order dated 30-08-2016 is not barred by limitation. Issue is decided in favor of 
the Petitioner. 


Issue No. III 


The perusal of record goes to reveal that in this claim petition, petitioner has challenged his dismissal order 
dated 27" May 2016 passed by Respondent Management on the grounds alleged in petition. Furthermore, perusal of 
the record of inquiry proceeding along with inquiry report, goes to reveal that the Petitioner was given fair 
opportunity of hearing at every stage of proceedings, which he availed, without raising any objection complaining of 
any prejudice of any nature caused to him before the inquiry officer at any point of time. Further, it is noticed that the 
Workman CSC received all the documents filed and relied upon by the Respondent management in support of the 
charge sheet, and CSC workman also filed a reply, cross-examined the management witnesses, and also examined 
himself as a witness in defense. Thus, the workman CSC has participated in the inquiry proceeding at every stage. 
Inquiry officer, on appreciation of evidence recorded in inquiry has submitted his reasoned report holding the 
workman guilty of the charges. Therefore, in the opinion of the court, no case is made out to hold that the domestic 
inquiry suffers from any procedural lapses or was conducted in violation of principles of natural justice, thereby 
causing any prejudice to the rights of the Petitioner. Moreover, validity and legality of the domestic inquiry has been 
upheld by the court vide order dated 11" November 2024. Thus, the plea of the Petitioner that the domestic inquiry 
was conducted against the Petitioner in violation of principle of natural justice is untenable. 


It is settled law that once it is held that the domestic inquiry is legal and proper, the next question arises for 
consideration whether the punishment imposed on the Petitioner is just and legal, or it is disproportionate to the 


7310 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


gravity of the charges. Petitioner has challenged his dismissal order on the ground that the allegations leveled against 
him are false and fabricated, and during the inquiry no other employee as witness was examined to prove the charges 
and there was no corroborating evidence to prove the guilt and only that management witness were examined in the 
inquiry. Further, it is contended that there was no legal evidence before enquiry to prove the allegations, and the 
inquiry officer had also failed to bring home the charge against the Petitioner. Further, Petitioner has strenuously 
argued that the inquiry officer conducted the inquiry as empty formality and without having any valid and legal 
evidence and came to the conclusion that allegations are proved. Further, it is urged Petitioner that had not committed 
any misconduct as alleged in the charge sheet, and there was no evidence of loss of revenue to the corporation. 
Further, it is contended that there was no willful insubordination or disobedience of instructions in connection with 
the orders of the superior. There was no damage or dishonesty in connection with the employer’s business or 
property, and Petitioner was not involved in unprovoked misbehavior with the customer, riotous, disorderly, or 
indecent behavior in the premises of the establishment. Lastly it is pleaded that the dismissal order passed by the 
Respondent management is grossly disproportionate to the gravity of the offense, and same is liable to be set aside. In 
view of plea taken by Petitioner, peruse the record of inquiry proceeding.

Ramprasad (MW8), and Mr. B. Vijay Sarathi Babu (MW9), and lastly, Mr. D. Veera swami (MW10). All the above 
stated witnesses, in their deposition have substantiated the allegations of the charge sheet issued against the CSC

his superiors. Furthermore, he threatened senior officials, displaying gross indiscipline and a blatant disregard for the 
hierarchical structure and decorum expected within the organization.

documentary proof. The enquiry was conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice, providing the

workman squarely fall under the category of serious misconduct as defined under Clauses 19(a), (c), (d) and (e) 
of the Andhra Pradesh Shops and establishments Rules, 1990.

Rules 19 (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of AP Shops & Establishment Rules provides as here under: - 

i. Clause 19(a): Willful insubordination or disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of a superior. 
ii. Clause 19(C): Damage to the employer’s property. 

iii. Clause 19(d): Riotous or disorderly behavior in the premises of the establishment. 

iv. Clause 19(e): Threatening or intimidating any employee or superior. 


The misconduct committed by the workman along with employees of assaulting superiors, instigating others, and 
participating in the riotous violent activities constitute serious act of misconduct which strike at the root of workplace 
discipline. The act of workman causing grievous injuries to managerial staff is a grave and serious misconduct that is 
not condonable. Therefore, the dismissal order passed by Respondent against the workman is justified and 
appropriate action. 


13. Respondent has relied upon the few decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court which are relevant to the point and 
discussed as here under: - 


(d) Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishnakali Tea Estate Bharatiya Vs. Aknn Chah Mazdoor Sanah - (2004) 8 SCC 
200 upheld the dismissal of workmen who had assaulted managerial personnel causing damage to property, 
gherao of the management, wrongfully confining manager. The Apex Court observed that such violent 
Conduct cannot be taken lightly, and the punishment of dismissal was warranted to preserve discipline and 
safety at the workplace. 


(e) Similarly, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Muriadih Colliery Vs. Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union - 
(2005) 3 SCC 331, held that the dismissal of employees who participated in a violent mob attack, causing 
injury to the General Manager, was justified, and interference by the Labour Court under Section 11-A of the 
ID Act was disapproved and the punishment proportionate to the misconduct. was upheld. 


(f) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M.P, Electricity Board Vs. Jagdish Chandra Sharma - order (2005) 
3 SCC 401. of dismissal of a Workman who assaulted a senior officer, restored the decision of the Industrial 
Court, thereby reiterating that acts of violence by employees, particularly against their superiors, must be 
dealt with strictly and are not open to lenient treatment. The reinstatement ordered by the Labour Court was 
reversed, affirming the employer's authority to maintain discipline through dismissal. 


(d) In the case of Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka - (2006) 1 


SSC 430, the Hon’ble Supreme Court underscored the importance of workplace discipline and held that even 
provoked assault on a superior, amounts to gross indiscipline. The Court stated: "30. In view of the change in 
economic policy of the country, it may not now be proper to allow the employees to break the discipline with 
impunity. Our country is governed by the rule of law. All actions, therefore, must be taken in accordance with 
law.” 


(f) In the case of Usha Breco Mazdoor Sangh Vs. Management of M/S. Usha Breco Ltd — (2008) 5 SCC 554, 
Hon’ble Supreme Court while reaffirming the legal position laid down by it is in the case firestone Tyre and 
Rubber Co. Vs. The management and Others — (1973) 1 SCC 813, held: - 


“31. It is one thing to say that finding of an Enquiry Officer is perverse or betrays the well-known doctrine of 
proportionality another thing to say that only because two views are possible, the Labour Court shall interfere 
therewith. In other words, it is one thing to say that on the basis of the materials on record, the Labour Court comes to 
a conclusion that a verdict of guilt has been arrived at by the Enquiry Officer whereas the materials suggested 
otherwise but it is another thing to say that such a verdict was also a possible view. 


39. The upshot of our discussion is that the decision of the labour Court should not be based on mere 
hypothesis. It cannot overturn a decision of the Management on ipse dixit. Its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the 
Act although is a wide one, must be judiciously exercise either whimsically or capriciously. It may scrutinize and 
analyze the evidence but what is important is how it does so.” 


(f) Further, in the case of New Shorrock Mills vs Maheshbhai T. Rao, 1996 SCC page 590. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court held: - 


“35. In the case of New Shorrock Mills Vs. (1996) Maheshbhai T Rao 6 of SCC 590, held that: 


"Labour Court in the present case having come to a Conclusion that the finding of the departmental enquiry was legal 
and proper, the Respondents order of discharge was not by way of victimization and that the Respondent workman 
had Seriously misbehaved and was thus guilty of misconduct, ought not to have interfered with the punishment, 
which was awarded, in the manner it did. This is not a case where the Court Could Come to the conclusion that the 
punishment was awarded was shockingly disproportionate to the employee's conduct and his past service record."
